modules.title: AR, MA, and ARIMA forecasting
modules.subtitle: Construct recursive forecasts and compare dynamic mean specifications with an explicit horizon and information set.
modules.objective: Construct recursive forecasts and compare dynamic mean specifications with an explicit horizon and information set.
modules.reading: Unit 3 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An autoregressive model relates the current value to earlier values; a moving-average model relates it to current and earlier innovations. The moving average in ARMA terminology is not a rolling average of prices. ARIMA adds differencing when an integrated component is part of the specification. Seasonal terms require a justified calendar period and enough cycles to estimate.

Forecasting propagates the estimated model from information available at the origin. Future innovations have conditional mean zero under the model but remain a source of forecast uncertainty. A point forecast should therefore be accompanied by a horizon-specific uncertainty statement and a comparison with a simple baseline.

$$
\hat y_{t+h|t}=\mu+\phi^h(y_t-\mu)
$$

## A worked example

Use y_t=.2+.8y_(t−1)+u_t with latest observation 2. The one-step prediction is 1.8; the two-step prediction is .2+.8×1.8=1.64. Both move toward the stationary mean 1. If innovation variance is .04 and parameters are treated as known, two-step forecast error variance is .04×(1+.8²)=.0656.

The random-walk baseline instead predicts the latest level 2 at both horizons. Whether the AR forecast improves matters empirically; mean reversion in a fitted equation is not proof of reliable future reversion.

## Implementation and interpretation

Choose candidate orders using development data and inspect residual dependence, convergence, stationarity, and invertibility conditions where relevant. Preserve the transformation needed to convert forecasts back to levels. Log the origin and horizon of every forecast; one-step rolling evaluation differs from a fixed-origin multi-step exercise. Never refresh a multi-step forecast with future observed values while labeling it as the original forecast.

modules.title: Forecast selection and rolling evaluation
modules.subtitle: Separate information criteria, development selection, and untouched evaluation, including overlapping forecast errors.
modules.objective: Separate information criteria, development selection, and untouched evaluation, including overlapping forecast errors.
modules.reading: Unit 3 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Information criteria trade in-sample likelihood fit against parameter complexity under a defined statistical model. They are not realized trading-performance scores. Comparing AIC or BIC requires compatible likelihoods and observations; a change in differencing or effective sample can complicate a naive comparison.

A rolling-origin evaluation repeatedly trains using only observations available at each origin and scores later outcomes. Expanding windows retain earlier history; rolling windows limit it. This choice changes the bias–variance and regime-adaptation trade-off. Hyperparameters must be selected inside the development process rather than repeatedly optimized on the final test period.

$$
AIC=2k-2\log\hat L
$$

## A worked example

Model A has log likelihood −100 and three estimated parameters, so AIC is 206. Model B has log likelihood −98 and six parameters, so AIC is 208. Under the same-data comparison, A is preferred by AIC even though B fits better.

Suppose forecast errors on a held-out segment are [1,−1,2]. MSE is 2 and MAE is 4/3. Squared loss places more weight on the large miss. For overlapping multi-step forecasts, adjacent errors share outcomes, so a comparison test must address dependence rather than count every row as independent.

## Implementation and interpretation

Save origin, training cutoff, label availability, chosen parameters, prediction, actual outcome, and baseline for every fold. Aggregate performance by horizon and regime as well as overall. Distinguish parameter-selection uncertainty from observation uncertainty. A difference in average loss should be paired with uncertainty suited to the forecast design; avoid declaring a universal winner from a handful of correlated errors.

modules.title: VAR systems and predictive causality
modules.subtitle: Model interdependent series while distinguishing Granger predictability from structural causal effects.
modules.objective: Model interdependent series while distinguishing Granger predictability from structural causal effects.
modules.reading: Unit 3 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A vector autoregression models each variable using lags of all included variables. It can capture feedback in predictive dynamics, but the parameter count grows with variables and lags. Stable estimation requires sufficient observations, appropriate transformations, and a coherent system specification.

A Granger-style restriction asks whether one variable's lagged values improve prediction of another conditional on the included information. It does not by itself establish an intervention effect. Omitted variables, timing differences, and contemporaneous shocks can create predictive relationships without the proposed economic causality.

$$
y_t=c+A_1y_{t-1}+u_t
$$

## A worked example

Let the next two-variable mean equal A times the current vector, where A has rows [.6,.2] and [.1,.5], and the current vector is [2,1]. Predictions are [1.4,.7]. An isolated shock of one unit to the first variable has next-step propagation [.6,.1] under this reduced-form dynamic map.

A structural impulse response additionally needs assumptions that identify economically meaningful shocks from correlated innovations. Cholesky ordering is one identification choice, not a fact discovered automatically from the covariance matrix.

## Implementation and interpretation

Inspect lag selection, residual autocorrelation, stability, deterministic terms, and available sample size. If levels are integrated and cointegrated, consider a system that preserves the long-run relation rather than blindly applying a stationary VAR to levels or discarding all information by differencing. Report the ordering or restrictions used in impulse responses and show sensitivity to plausible alternatives. Keep the language predictive unless a structural identification argument has been supplied.

modules.title: Time series and cointegration
modules.subtitle: Test whether integrated series share a stable long-run combination and distinguish that evidence from a tradable spread.
modules.objective: Test whether integrated series share a stable long-run combination and distinguish that evidence from a tradable spread.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Cointegration describes integrated variables whose particular linear combination is stationary under the chosen definition and deterministic terms. High correlation alone is insufficient: two unrelated trending series can look strongly associated. Establish plausible integration orders and an economic relation before testing a residual combination.

In a two-step Engle–Granger procedure, first estimate a levels relation and then assess its residual stationarity using the appropriate cointegration test distribution. Ordinary standalone ADF critical values are not automatically valid for estimated residuals. The null of the usual cointegration test is no cointegration under its assumptions.

$$
s_t=y_t-\alpha-\beta x_t
$$

## A worked example

Suppose the estimated relation is y=2+1.5x+s. At x=10 and y=18, the estimated spread residual is 1. A change of units from x dollars to x cents changes the numerical hedge coefficient; the economic exposure must be converted consistently. If the two levels are both I(1) and the residual process is stationary, the relation may be cointegrating.

Even with that statistical evidence, fees, borrow constraints, adjustment delays, parameter uncertainty, and structural breaks can make a spread strategy unattractive. The in-app long/cash simulator cannot represent a simultaneous long/short pair.

## Implementation and interpretation

Fit the relation on a training interval and assess stability on later data. Keep the intercept/trend convention, lag selection, test null, and estimated hedge units in the report. Inspect a known break and compare rolling estimates. Never select hundreds of pairs and interpret the smallest unadjusted p-value as a prespecified discovery. Preserve the distinction between evidence for a long-run relation and evidence for an executable after-cost strategy.

modules.title: Error correction and adjustment speed
modules.subtitle: Interpret an error-correction coefficient and calculate a model-dependent spread half-life.
modules.objective: Interpret an error-correction coefficient and calculate a model-dependent spread half-life.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An error-correction model links short-run changes to lagged deviation from a long-run relation, often with additional lagged differences. A negative adjustment coefficient can describe correction when the spread is above its equilibrium, but sign conventions and the variable being modeled matter. In a multivariate system, more than one variable may adjust.

For a simple AR(1) spread s_t=phi*s_(t−1)+u_t with 0<phi<1, the half-life is log(.5)/log(phi). This is a property of a fitted linear conditional-mean model. It is not a guaranteed exit time, and the expression needs modification or a different interpretation for oscillatory, unit-root, or explosive dynamics.

$$
h_{1/2}=\log(0.5)/\log(\phi)
$$

## A worked example

A spread coefficient phi=.8 implies a half-life of about 3.106 observation periods. In the corresponding difference equation, delta s_t=−.2*s_(t−1)+u_t. If the previous spread is 5, the expected next change is −1 and the expected next level is 4.

Daily and weekly observations give different calendar interpretations of the same numeric half-life. Parameter uncertainty is also nonlinear near phi=1: a small estimation change can greatly increase the inferred horizon.

## Implementation and interpretation

Estimate adjustment dynamics only after a defensible long-run specification. Report the sampling frequency, coefficient interval, residual diagnostics, and sensitivity across regimes. Define exits using both model evidence and operational risk; do not wait indefinitely because a fitted half-life once looked short. The worked worksheet uses fixed parameters; the downloadable lab estimates an autoregression from a synthetic spread and exposes its limitations.

print("Spread half-life:", math.log(0.5) / math.log(0.8))
print("Expected spread change:", -0.2 * 5)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

assignment.solution: Half-life is one observation period and the next conditional mean is 4. Realized shocks, changing parameters, and execution constraints can prevent the expected path and any intended exit.

modules.title: ARCH, GARCH, and volatility persistence
modules.subtitle: Model conditional variance separately from the return mean and evaluate the restrictions behind a long-run variance.
modules.objective: Model conditional variance separately from the return mean and evaluate the restrictions behind a long-run variance.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Volatility clustering means large absolute returns tend to occur near other large absolute returns. A conditional-variance model allows forecast uncertainty to evolve even when expected returns remain near a constant. ARCH uses lagged squared innovations; GARCH also includes lagged conditional variance to represent persistence parsimoniously.

In the standard GARCH(1,1) recursion, nonnegative omega, alpha, and beta with omega positive provide common positivity conditions. Under the usual innovation and finite-second-moment setup, alpha+beta<1 gives a finite unconditional variance omega/(1−alpha−beta). These conditions do not establish a correct tail distribution or guarantee useful forecasts.

$$
h_t=\omega+\alpha u_{t-1}^2+\beta h_{t-1}
$$

## A worked example

Let omega=.01, alpha=.1, beta=.8, previous squared innovation .09, and previous variance .04. The next variance is .01+.1×.09+.8×.04=.051, with standard deviation about .2258 in the chosen return units. Persistence is .9 and the model's unconditional variance is .1.

If returns are changed from decimals to percentage points, squared-return quantities and omega scale by 10,000. Mixing an omega estimated on percentages with decimal inputs produces a seriously incorrect variance path.

## Implementation and interpretation

Separate parameter estimation from recursion with stipulated parameters. Inspect optimizer convergence, parameter restrictions, standardized residuals, remaining squared-residual dependence, and sensitivity to innovation distribution. Compare forecasts on later data against a simple rolling-variance or EWMA baseline. The course project computes transparent fixed-parameter recursions; optional estimation with the arch package requires a separately specified environment and convergence review.

import math
h = 0.01 + 0.1 * 0.09 + 0.8 * 0.04
print("GARCH next variance:", h)
print("GARCH next volatility:", math.sqrt(h))
print("Long-run variance:", 0.01 / (1 - 0.1 - 0.8))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

assignment.solution: Next variance is .086. Alpha+beta=.9, so the usual unconditional variance is .02/.1=.2. Both are in squared return units, not return units.

modules.title: Asymmetry, fat tails, and variance forecast loss
modules.subtitle: Evaluate asymmetric volatility responses and compare positive variance forecasts without confusing fit with tail calibration.
modules.objective: Evaluate asymmetric volatility responses and compare positive variance forecasts without confusing fit with tail calibration.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A symmetric squared-shock model responds equally to positive and negative innovations of the same magnitude. GJR-style terms allow an additional response to negative shocks under a specified indicator convention. EGARCH models log variance with a different functional form. These are alternative models, not automatic upgrades for every asset or sampling frequency.

A heavy-tailed innovation distribution changes likelihood and tail probabilities; it does not mean all relevant moments exist. Distinguish a conditional scale from an unconditional tail measure. Validate residual and forecast behavior rather than choosing a distribution only because it improves training likelihood.

$$
QLIKE(h,v)=\log(h)+v/h,\quad h>0
$$

## A worked example

Consider a GJR addition gamma*u² for a negative innovation, with gamma=.2 and magnitude .3. Relative to an equally sized positive shock, the negative shock adds .2×.09=.018 variance units. Positivity and stationarity restrictions depend on the full specification and innovation distribution.

For positive variance forecast h=.04 and realized variance proxy v=.09, a common QLIKE form is log(h)+v/h, approximately −.9689. Its absolute value may be negative; comparisons on the same observations matter. A squared-return proxy is noisy, and loss interpretation depends on the proxy's properties.

## Implementation and interpretation

Evaluate variance forecasts at a consistent horizon and scale, with a baseline and a frozen test interval. Use multiple diagnostics: likelihood, variance loss, standardized residuals, and tail-exceedance behavior. A good average variance forecast can still misrepresent extreme losses. Explain whether parameters were estimated or stipulated and how zero or nonpositive variance forecasts are rejected before taking logarithms or dividing.

print("QLIKE forecast loss:", math.log(0.04) + 0.09 / 0.04)

modules.subtitle: Specify factor exposures with consistent excess-return units and distinguish explanatory loadings from expected risk premiums.
modules.objective: Specify factor exposures with consistent excess-return units and distinguish explanatory loadings from expected risk premiums.
modules.reading: Unit 5 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A time-series factor regression relates an asset's excess return to common return factors. In CAPM form, the market excess return is the regressor. Multi-factor extensions include portfolios constructed to represent additional characteristics or risks. Factor definitions, universe, rebalancing, and data revisions are part of the model, not interchangeable labels.

A time-series loading measures exposure to a factor's realized return variation. An expected factor premium is a different quantity, estimated with substantial uncertainty. A factor that explains covariance does not automatically earn a stable positive premium. Check whether the factor series are already excess returns or long–short spreads before subtracting a risk-free rate again.

$$
r_{i,t}-r_{f,t}=\alpha_i+\beta_i^\top f_t+\epsilon_{i,t}
$$

## A worked example

Cedar uses alpha=.001, market loading 1.1, size loading .3, and value loading −.2, all with returns in decimals. For factor returns .02, .01, and −.005, the fitted excess return is .001+.022+.003+.001=.027, or 2.7%. A realized asset excess return of .03 leaves residual .003.

Negative value exposure describes this conditional regression loading. It is not proof that the portfolio follows a particular manager intention, and it can change with holdings or factor definitions.

## Implementation and interpretation

Document factor construction from the primary data provider and align the same dates and currency conventions. Report alpha, loadings, robust uncertainty, sample fit, and stability. In Quanta's factor studio, seeded synthetic factors have planted relationships and are labeled accordingly; they are not historical Fama–French observations. Uploaded observations must match the chosen model columns exactly. Replicate coefficient calculations before interpreting investment skill.

modules.title: Alpha inference, attribution, and changing exposure
modules.subtitle: Separate realized factor contributions, residual returns, statistical alpha, and evidence of repeatable performance.
modules.objective: Separate realized factor contributions, residual returns, statistical alpha, and evidence of repeatable performance.
modules.reading: Unit 5 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A realized factor contribution is a loading multiplied by a factor return under a specified attribution model. Summing contributions and residuals reconciles a modeled period's return; it does not prove that the same exposures or premiums will persist. Holdings-based and return-based attribution use different information and can disagree.

Regression alpha is conditional on the included factors, frequency, sample, and accounting conventions. An omitted factor, nonlinear exposure, stale pricing, or selection can create apparent alpha. Statistical uncertainty, multiple testing, economic costs, and stability matter before interpreting it as skill.

$$
r_t=\sum_j\beta_j f_{j,t}+\epsilon_t
$$

## A worked example

A period's market contribution is 1.5%, size contribution −.2%, value contribution .3%, and residual .4%. Total explained-plus-residual return is 2%. The residual is not automatically a persistent 0.4% monthly alpha.

A daily intercept estimate .0002 with HAC standard error .00015 has statistic about 1.333. Multiplying both by 252 changes reporting scale but leaves this ratio unchanged; it does not create more independent evidence or provide a correctly compounded annual return forecast.

## Implementation and interpretation

Compare rolling or expanding exposure estimates and retain their windows. An unstable coefficient may reflect changing holdings, weak identification, or noisy estimates. Use economic explanations and uncertainty to interpret changes rather than reacting to every wiggle. Evaluate any selected alpha on untouched later observations, with benchmark costs and all tried variants logged. Avoid mixing additive arithmetic attribution with compounded multi-period returns without an explicit linking convention.

modules.title: Portfolio theory and factor pricing
modules.subtitle: Compute covariance-driven portfolio risk and distinguish an optimizer's in-sample solution from a robust allocation.
modules.objective: Compute covariance-driven portfolio risk and distinguish an optimizer's in-sample solution from a robust allocation.
modules.reading: Unit 5 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Portfolio variance depends on weights, individual variances, and cross-asset covariances. Diversification can reduce risk when returns are imperfectly correlated, but does not guarantee positive returns or protection in every crisis. Correlations and volatilities are estimates that can change together under stress.

Mean–variance optimization chooses weights under an estimated objective and constraints. Small changes in expected returns or covariance can produce large weight changes, particularly near singularity or with unconstrained leverage. Constraints encode a mandate; they also change the solution and should be reported explicitly.

$$
\sigma_p^2=w^\top\Sigma w
$$

## A worked example

Two assets have annualized volatilities 20% and 10%, correlation .3, and equal weights. Variance is .25×.04+.25×.01+2×.5×.5×.3×.2×.1=.0155, so volatility is about 12.45%. If correlation rises to 1 with the other inputs unchanged, volatility becomes 15%.

A portfolio can therefore lose diversification benefit without any change in nominal weights. A lower-correlation estimate is useful only to the extent it represents the relevant future conditions and comparable measurement conventions.

## Implementation and interpretation

Audit covariance symmetry, positive semidefiniteness, data units, and sample overlap before optimization. Compare equal weighting, a simple constrained minimum-variance portfolio, and stress scenarios. Separate expected return assumptions from realized evaluation. Quanta's optimizer uses long-only constraints and disclosed shrinkage; its output is an in-sample estimated allocation, not a recommendation proven best for future markets.

modules.title: Shrinkage, PCA, and estimation risk
modules.subtitle: Regularize noisy covariance estimates and distinguish statistical components from economically named factors.
modules.objective: Regularize noisy covariance estimates and distinguish statistical components from economically named factors.
modules.reading: Unit 5 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Sample covariance becomes unstable when the number of assets is large relative to observations, or when assets are highly redundant. Shrinkage blends it with a structured target. The target and intensity express a trade-off between sample detail and stability; they are not universal constants. Estimate or choose them within development data and report sensitivity.

Principal components find orthogonal directions of sample variation. A leading component may resemble a market factor, but its sign is arbitrary and its economic meaning is not supplied by the algorithm. Explained variance measures reconstruction of variation, not expected profit or causal importance.

$$
\hat\Sigma_{shrink}=(1-\lambda)S+\lambda T
$$

## A worked example

A sample covariance has diagonal entries .04 and .01 and off-diagonal .018. Shrinking 50% toward its diagonal target leaves variances unchanged and reduces covariance to .009. Equal-weight variance changes from .0215 to .017. The lower estimated number is a consequence of the chosen model, not proof that actual future risk fell.

If covariance eigenvalues are .06, .03, and .01, the first principal component explains 60% of total sample variance. Retaining it discards 40%, which may include economically important risks.

## Implementation and interpretation

Fit normalization and components on training data, then transform later observations using the frozen artifact. Inspect component stability and factor interpretation across windows. Report the shrinkage target, intensity, asset order, and units. Compare realized risk of constrained allocations against simple baselines rather than choosing the estimator solely because it gives the lowest in-sample volatility.

print("Equal-weight shrunk variance:", 0.25 * 0.04 + 0.25 * 0.01 + 0.5 * covariance)

modules.title: Panel data, fixed effects, and clustered inference
modules.subtitle: Separate within-entity from between-entity variation and match covariance estimation to panel dependence.
modules.objective: Separate within-entity from between-entity variation and match covariance estimation to panel dependence.
modules.reading: Unit 6 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Panel data observe entities repeatedly over time. Entity fixed effects absorb time-invariant entity-specific components, so coefficients are identified from within-entity variation after the chosen transformation and other controls. Time effects absorb common date-specific components. A time-invariant regressor cannot be separately estimated alongside unrestricted entity effects.

Fixed effects do not automatically remove time-varying confounding, reverse causality, measurement error, or dynamic-panel bias. Random effects add assumptions about the relationship between entity components and regressors. Choose the model according to the estimand and defensible assumptions rather than whichever produces a smaller p-value.

$$
y_{it}-\bar y_i=\beta(x_{it}-\bar x_i)+(u_{it}-\bar u_i)
$$

## A worked example

Firm A has x=[1,2] and y=[3,5]; firm B has x=[3,4] and y=[10,12]. Demeaning within each firm gives x deviations [−.5,.5] and y deviations [−1,1] for both. The within slope is 2. The level differences between firms are absorbed by their intercepts.

Repeated observations within a firm may share disturbances. An entity-clustered covariance allows certain within-cluster dependence under its assumptions, but a tiny number of clusters provides weak asymptotic support. Two firms here demonstrate arithmetic, not reliable clustered inference.

## Implementation and interpretation

Check panel keys, duplicate entity-date rows, missing histories, and the source of identifying variation. Report entity/time effects, covariance clusters, and the number of independent clusters. Consider common shocks and two-way clustering when justified, with appropriate finite-sample care. Explain whether the question concerns within-firm changes or cross-firm differences; fixed effects can answer a different question from a pooled regression.

modules.title: Instrumental variables and two-stage least squares
modules.subtitle: Explain relevance, exclusion, and instrument exogeneity and interpret a simple IV estimate with weak-instrument caution.
modules.objective: Explain relevance, exclusion, and instrument exogeneity and interpret a simple IV estimate with weak-instrument caution.
modules.reading: Unit 6 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An instrument offers variation in an endogenous regressor that can support identification under explicit assumptions. Relevance links the instrument to the regressor after controls. Exclusion and exogeneity require that the instrument not affect the structural outcome through an omitted direct route or correlated disturbance, under the proposed model. These assumptions require substantive evidence; a strong first stage alone does not prove validity.

Two-stage least squares projects endogenous regressors onto instruments and exogenous controls, then estimates the structural relationship using the projected variation. Correct IV covariance accounts for this procedure. Naively treating fitted regressors as ordinary observed variables can give incorrect uncertainty.

$$
\hat\beta_{IV}=\widehat{Cov}(z,y)/\widehat{Cov}(z,x)
$$

## A worked example

In a centered single-instrument setup, covariance between z and y is .6 and between z and x is .3, so the simple IV slope is 2. If the denominator were .03, the ratio would be 20, illustrating sensitivity to weak first-stage variation. This arithmetic does not identify a universal weak-instrument threshold.

An overidentification test, when available, assesses certain joint restrictions under assumptions. Passing it does not prove every instrument is valid, and exactly identified models lack that overidentifying comparison.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write an instrument argument covering timing, mechanism, exclusion threats, and the population affected. Report first-stage diagnostics, the instrument set, controls, covariance convention, and weak-instrument-robust inference when appropriate. Do not select instruments only because they produce the desired structural coefficient. Compare ordinary and IV estimates as evidence to interpret, not as an automatic instruction to trust whichever is larger.

modules.subtitle: Calculate a two-group treatment contrast and identify the counterfactual assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.
modules.objective: Calculate a two-group treatment contrast and identify the counterfactual assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.
modules.reading: Unit 6 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Difference-in-differences compares outcome changes across treated and comparison groups. In the basic design, the untreated potential outcome trend for the treated group must be credibly represented by the comparison group's trend, conditional on the specified assumptions. Stable composition, no anticipatory response, and limited spillovers may also matter.

A pre-trend graph is useful but cannot prove the counterfactual parallel-trends assumption. Few pre-periods or noisy estimates can conceal relevant differences. Event-study coefficients require a reference period and a clear treatment-timing convention. With staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, a naive two-way fixed-effects coefficient can combine comparisons in misleading ways.

$$
DiD=(\bar y_{T,post}-\bar y_{T,pre})-(\bar y_{C,post}-\bar y_{C,pre})
$$

## A worked example

The treated group's mean outcome rises from 10 to 14; the comparison group rises from 8 to 10. The difference-in-differences contrast is (14−10)−(10−8)=2. The raw treated change of 4 includes the shared change represented by the control group.

If a separate industry shock affects only treated entities at the treatment date, the contrast can include that shock as well as treatment. More precise standard errors do not repair the missing counterfactual.

## Implementation and interpretation

Specify treatment timing, eligible comparison entities, outcome measurement, and pre-period diagnostics before estimating. Match inference to the level of treatment assignment and dependence. Investigate anticipation, spillovers, and concurrent policies; show transparent group-time patterns. For staggered designs, use an estimator whose comparisons match the intended effect and heterogeneity assumptions. Report the descriptive contrast separately when causal assumptions are not credible.

modules.title: Binary outcomes, likelihood, and probability forecasts
modules.subtitle: Interpret logistic models and marginal effects while separating event probability from economic payoff.
modules.objective: Interpret logistic models and marginal effects while separating event probability from economic payoff.
modules.reading: Unit 6 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A binary outcome model specifies a probability rather than an unrestricted linear mean. Logistic regression maps a linear index through the logistic function, keeping fitted probabilities between zero and one. Coefficients are changes in log odds conditional on the included terms; they are not constant changes in probability.

Maximum likelihood estimates parameters by evaluating how plausible the observed outcomes are under the model. Separation, rare events, dependence, and misspecification can impair estimates and uncertainty. Class weighting or oversampling changes the fitting objective and can require careful probability recalibration before deployment.

$$
p(x)=1/(1+e^{-x^\top\beta})
$$

## A worked example

A linear index of zero gives probability .5. Increasing it to log(3) gives probability .75 because the odds are three to one. With slope .8 at probability .5, the local derivative with respect to x is .8×.5×.5=.2 per unit of x under this simple specification. The derivative changes at other baseline probabilities.

A .75 probability of a gain does not establish positive expected profit if losses are much larger than gains or costs consume the advantage. Predicting event frequency and deciding an allocation are separate problems.

## Implementation and interpretation

State the event definition, horizon, label availability, class prevalence, and decision threshold. Evaluate calibration, discrimination, proper scoring losses, and economic decision costs on later data. Inspect separation and convergence warnings rather than accepting enormous coefficients at face value. If repeated entity observations are used, choose an inference or predictive evaluation design that acknowledges their dependence.

modules.subtitle: Define empirical quantiles, expected shortfall, drawdown, and exceedance checks with explicit signs and horizons.
modules.objective: Define empirical quantiles, expected shortfall, drawdown, and exceedance checks with explicit signs and horizons.
modules.reading: Unit 7 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Risk measures summarize different features of a return or loss distribution. Value at Risk is a quantile under a specified horizon and probability convention; it is not the largest possible loss. Expected shortfall summarizes losses in an explicitly defined tail. Maximum drawdown is a path-dependent peak-to-trough decline, so rearranging the same returns can change it.

Finite samples make quantile conventions important. Interpolation, tied observations, and whether a threshold observation belongs to the tail can change the reported estimate. Use a documented convention and avoid representing a few historical observations as precise tail probabilities. Conditional and unconditional risk forecasts also answer different questions.

$$
DD_t=E_t/\max_{s\leq t}E_s-1
$$

## A worked example

A portfolio peaks at 200 and falls to 150, giving drawdown 150/200−1=−25%. Recovering from 150 to 200 requires a 33.33% gain because the return denominator changed.

Take ordered losses [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,20]. Under the nearest-rank 90% quantile convention, VaR is the ninth observation, 9. Under a deliberately defined strictly-above-threshold tail, the mean is 20. Including the threshold would give 14.5; neither convention should be hidden behind an unexplained ES label.

## Implementation and interpretation

State loss signs, horizon, confidence level, sample size, quantile method, and tail inclusion rule. For a forecast, inspect exceedance frequency and clustering; a correct average count can hide failures concentrated during crises. Compare model risk with scenario analysis and liquidity constraints. A drawdown stop is an operating rule, not proof that realized losses cannot exceed the selected threshold.

modules.title: Bootstrap uncertainty under dependence
modules.subtitle: Choose a resampling unit that preserves relevant dependence and interpret bootstrap intervals within their assumptions.
modules.objective: Choose a resampling unit that preserves relevant dependence and interpret bootstrap intervals within their assumptions.
modules.reading: Unit 7 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A bootstrap approximates an estimator's sampling behavior by resampling according to a declared mechanism. Independent row resampling is appropriate only when its independence approximation is defensible. Financial observations can be serially dependent, cross-sectionally linked, or grouped by entity, making the resampling unit central to the analysis.

A moving-block bootstrap samples contiguous blocks to retain some local serial structure. Block length trades preservation of dependence against the effective number of independently drawn blocks. Very short blocks may erase dependence; very long blocks produce few distinct resamples. Structural changes and heavy tails can also limit a naive bootstrap interpretation.

$$
\hat\theta^{*(b)}=T(Data^{*(b)})
$$

## A worked example

A 12-observation series is grouped into blocks of length three. Drawing four blocks yields a 12-observation resample under the chosen concatenation rule. Sampling individual rows would discard their within-block order. If overlapping blocks are allowed, possible starting positions and end handling must be specified.

For illustrative bootstrap estimates [.1,.2,.3,.4,.5], a nearest-rank 20% and 80% interval uses .1 and .4. This tiny set demonstrates quantile indexing only; a practical interval needs many draws and a justified resampling model.

## Implementation and interpretation

Set and record the random seed, block rule, number of draws, statistic, and interval method. Refit the full estimation procedure in each draw when that matches the target uncertainty; resampling only already fitted residual summaries can omit estimation steps. Compare block lengths and assess sensitivity. Never describe a bootstrap interval as distribution-free proof of future trading performance.

modules.title: Multiple testing and selection bias
modules.subtitle: Account for a family of research attempts and distinguish family-wise error control from false-discovery control.
modules.objective: Account for a family of research attempts and distinguish family-wise error control from false-discovery control.
modules.reading: Unit 7 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Testing many variants creates opportunities for chance significance. The research family includes abandoned features, alternative universes, thresholds, samples, and model choices when they influenced selection. Reporting only the winner conceals the selection process. An untouched evaluation period helps, but repeatedly looking at it turns it into development data.

Bonferroni controls a family-wise error bound by dividing the family error level by the number of valid tests; it can be conservative, especially with dependent tests. False-discovery procedures target a different quantity and have their own dependence assumptions. Neither procedure repairs invalid individual p-values, data leakage, or an incorrectly defined research family.

$$
\alpha_{individual}=\alpha_{family}/m
$$

## A worked example

With 20 tests and family level .05, a Bonferroni threshold is .0025. A smallest raw p-value .01 is not significant under that rule, even though it is below .05. Under independence, the chance of at least one false rejection from twenty true nulls tested at .05 is 1−.95²⁰, about 64.15%.

This independence calculation is illustrative. Correlated strategy variants require more care; the observed number of trials is not automatically the number of independent trials, and hiding correlated trials is not a valid correction.

## Implementation and interpretation

Keep a research ledger with hypotheses, dates, tried variants, outcomes, and selection decisions. Predefine a small confirmatory family when possible, separate exploration from confirmation, and report effect sizes and uncertainty after selection. A deflated Sharpe or reality-check approach has additional distributional and dependence inputs; do not substitute a made-up trial discount for the specified method. Evaluate the chosen executable rule with costs after statistical selection.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An econometric finding becomes a strategy hypothesis only after specifying how information turns into decisions and fills. A signal calculated from a completed close cannot execute at an earlier open. A historical universe assembled from today's survivors can exclude failed firms. Revised financial data can leak information that was unavailable at the original decision date.

Separate an effect estimate, a forecast, a portfolio rule, and an execution model. Each adds assumptions. A regression's positive coefficient does not specify a holding period, turnover budget, position size, or liquidity constraint. Keep these transformations explicit and evaluate the complete frozen rule on later observations.

$$
r_{net}\approx r_{gross}-Turnover\times Cost_{one\ way}
$$

## A worked example

A gross strategy result is 8% over a stipulated period. Six one-way portfolio turnovers at 20 bps each consume 1.2%, leaving an approximate 6.8% before other omitted costs. If turnover rises to 20 equivalents, the same cost convention consumes 4%, leaving 4%. This additive approximation is a teaching decomposition; an actual ledger compounds dated cash flows and fees.

A close signal with price 100 may first fill at a next open of 103. Using 100 because it makes the historical curve smoother can materially overstate performance.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write a preregistration-style record: data provenance, availability, transformation code, split manifests, model choice, target mapping, costs, fills, benchmark, and rejected variants. Preserve seeds and package versions for reproducibility. Stress an alternative fee model, delayed execution, missing data, and a market regime change. State the weakest assumption and a test that could falsify it. The capstone combines statistical inference with this operational evidence rather than accepting a chart alone.

It estimates the levels relation, reports an Engle–Granger test, and fits simple spread dynamics. ## Model and assumptions

The local research project includes an explicit GARCH recursion with stipulated parameters and a covariance-shrinkage comparison. These components calculate model implications; they do not estimate GARCH parameters or prove that an optimized portfolio will outperform. Keep estimation, forecasting, allocation, and execution as separate artifacts.

A useful risk review examines the same holdings under several plausible input models. Compare sample covariance, a disclosed structured target, and a correlation stress. Report how concentration and expected turnover change when the allocation responds to those estimates. A lower model variance may simply reflect a more optimistic assumption.

$$
\hat\sigma_p=\sqrt{w^\top\hat\Sigma w}

## A worked example

Two equal-weight assets have variances .04 and .09 and covariance .018. Portfolio variance is .0415. Shrinking covariance halfway toward zero gives .009 and estimated variance .037. For an independent volatility check, omega=.01, alpha=.1, beta=.8, squared shock .04, and prior variance .09 give next variance .086. The number is a conditional estimate in squared units, not a maximum possible return loss.

Verify positive variance forecasts before computing loss metrics. Submit a review memo that distinguishes a changed estimate from a changed actual portfolio and states what evidence would justify altering a trading risk budget.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Choose one primary question: a conditional factor explanation, a dated forecast, a long-run relation, or a credible causal contrast. State the estimand and avoid combining these into an undefined claim of alpha. Assemble the data dictionary, as-of rules, model specification, diagnostics, covariance convention, selection history, and independent evaluation.

Run the downloadable project as a reproducibility baseline and add one self-designed sensitivity or negative-control experiment. All default data are synthetic. A later study using real observations needs a lawful data source, point-in-time metadata, and its own evaluation; changing the dataset is not a cosmetic substitution.

$$
R^2_{OOS}=1-MSE_{model}/MSE_{baseline}
$$

## A worked example

Cedar reports a coefficient .4 with HAC standard error .25, a large-sample interval [−.09,.89], and model MSE .8 against baseline MSE 1. The conditional prediction improvement is 20% under that loss comparison, while the parameter interval includes zero. Neither fact alone establishes a causal effect or a profitable strategy.

The study must explain how these different evidence types relate to its original question. If the model used realized future factor returns, its conditional explanatory task cannot silently become an ex-ante trading forecast.

## Implementation and interpretation

Self-assess 100 points: question and estimand 15, data/provenance 20, estimation and diagnostics 20, uncertainty and selection 20, independent evaluation 15, and reproducibility/decision memo 10. Require at least 80 and no unresolved information leak, unit inconsistency, invalid inference convention, or misrepresented data source. The automatic final assesses conceptual transfer; it does not grade the written dossier or certify a real-world investment result. Conclude with the strongest supported claim, the largest unresolved limitation, and the next falsifying experiment.

modules.content:
## The idea

Build a universe at each rebalance date, select the latest statements actually published, and compute per-share net-current-asset value. A price below two-thirds of NCAV is a candidate screen, not a complete investment decision.

$$
P_t<\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{NCAV}_t
$$

## A worked example

A stock at $6 with NCAV of $12 passes the valuation screen. If operating earnings are negative and quarterly cash burn is $2 per share, the apparent cushion can disappear quickly. Apply financial quality and liquidity filters before sizing.

## Research protocol

Use delisted securities and historical share counts. Compare gross and net performance, report turnover, and stress forced liquidation. The bundled synthetic data illustrates execution mechanics, not historical net-net profitability.

### In the sandbox

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. All default price paths are synthetic, and the accompanying trend strategy demonstrates execution mechanics. Its returns do not validate the lesson’s valuation thesis.

## The idea

Standardize earnings yield, invested-capital returns, and coverage within a contemporaneous universe. A composite score expresses an explicit preference rather than discovering an objective ranking. Avoid scale differences dominating the combination.

$$
\mathrm{Score}_i=\tfrac13[z(E/P)_i+z(ROIC)_i+z(\mathrm{Coverage})_i]
$$

## A worked example

Suppose a company’s standardized scores are 1.2 for earnings yield, 0.6 for ROIC, and −0.3 for coverage. Its equal-weight composite is 0.5. A debt-heavy company may look cheap on P/E while failing the coverage test.

## Research protocol

Winsorize using training-universe thresholds and neutralize sector exposures only if the thesis requires it. Track accounting definitions and compare with a simple equal-weight baseline.

modules.title: Statistical arbitrage pairs
modules.subtitle: Trade a spread with explicit exit conditions
modules.content:
## The idea

A pairs strategy trades deviations in a statistically justified spread. Estimate a hedge ratio and a spread mean and scale from past observations. Entry and exit thresholds must be set before observing the test-period outcome.

$$
z_t=\frac{s_t-\overline{s}_{t-L:t-1}}{\sigma_{s,t-L:t-1}}
$$

## A worked example

A spread of 8 with a trailing mean of 2 and standard deviation of 3 has z = 2. A mean-reversion rule might short the spread, while a risk rule exits if the relationship breaks. Hedging notional value alone does not ensure beta or dollar neutrality.

## Research protocol

Include short borrow, both legs’ commissions, and asynchronous fill risk. Re-estimate with a walk-forward schedule. Never assume that a historically stationary spread cannot undergo a permanent change.

### In the sandbox

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. All default price paths are synthetic, and the accompanying trend strategy demonstrates execution mechanics. Its returns do not validate the lesson’s valuation thesis.

modules.subtitle: Predict with a chronological research design
modules.content:
## The idea

Train regularized models on features known at prediction time. Cross-sectional ranking may be more stable than forecasting exact returns. The target horizon determines the embargo and overlap handling required between train and test sets.

$$
\widehat{\beta}=\arg\min_\beta\left\{\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2\right\}
$$

## A worked example

A 20-day forward return label for a training observation on January 31 contains February prices. A test fold beginning February 1 overlaps that information. Purge overlapping labels and apply an embargo appropriate to the design.

## Research protocol

Fit scaling and feature selection on training data only. Compare ridge and tree models with simple factor ranks. Report net turnover-adjusted outcomes and every material hyperparameter search.

### In the sandbox

modules.objective: Turn an investment idea into a testable decision contract with explicit data, execution, and failure assumptions.
modules.reading: Start here. Deliverable: a bot decision contract. Read the project guide, then complete the data and event units before designing a trading rule.
modules.content:
## Define the operation

A bot is a process that turns observations into state changes. Start with a decision contract: eligible instruments, information cutoff, signal rule, target holdings, rebalance frequency, execution convention, risk budget, and conditions for doing nothing. A slogan such as buy strong companies leaves almost every engineering choice unresolved.

Distinguish an alpha model from an execution algorithm. The first proposes which exposure might be useful. The second tries to obtain an already chosen exposure under trading constraints. A good execution algorithm does not establish predictive edge; a useful signal does not guarantee affordable fills.

The course follows a fictional Harbor research team building a long-only paper system. Dollar amounts, thresholds, and model outputs are stipulated teaching inputs. Each lesson produces one artifact for the final design dossier. Small calculations run in the in-app sandbox; the downloadable Python project runs an offline event and ledger simulation.

$$
\text{Net edge}_{bps}=\text{gross edge}-\text{spread}-\text{fees}-\text{slippage}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor proposes a daily strategy in a $100,000 paper portfolio. It may allocate at most 10% to one eligible stock, observes completed daily bars, and places a target order at the next eligible open. An estimate of 12 basis points of gross benefit faces 4 basis points of spread cost, 2 of fees, and 3 of slippage. The rough expected net benefit is only 3 basis points.

A second analyst assumes 6 basis points of slippage. That consumes the entire gross estimate. Before building a faster bot, the team must decide whether the underlying idea survives a plausible cost range. An estimate is not a realized return, and these cost components must not overlap.

## Acceptance evidence

Write observable requirements: duplicate delivery does not duplicate exposure; missing features produce no new order; a fill changes cash exactly once; a restart recovers a halted state. Pair each requirement with a normal and adverse example. Define success in terms of reconciliation and sound evaluation before looking at a profit chart.

Keep research permission, paper execution, and any later live release as separate stages. Completing this course produces a tested educational prototype and a review packet. It does not silently connect credentials or authorize a brokerage trade.

modules.reading: Deliverable: event schema and architecture diagram. Broker reference: stable client identifiers and order lookup; implementation semantics must be verified per adapter.
modules.content:
## Design a pipeline with explicit boundaries

Market ingestion records an observation. Feature computation produces a dated input set. Strategy logic proposes a target. Risk logic permits, resizes, or rejects that target. An order manager tracks instructions, and a fill handler updates the ledger. These steps can live in one process initially while retaining separate interfaces.

A vectorized research calculation is useful for rapid experiments; an event-driven replay is useful for modeling chronology and operational state. Neither architecture automatically prevents look-ahead. Both require correct timestamps and information boundaries.

Give each event a stable identity, source, event time, receipt time, and schema version. Event time describes the underlying observation; receipt time describes when the bot learned about it. A late event should follow a documented policy rather than revise a decision as if the data had arrived earlier.

$$
\text{Observation}\rightarrow\text{Features}\rightarrow\text{Target}\rightarrow\text{Risk}\rightarrow\text{Order}\rightarrow\text{Fill}
$$

## A worked example

The feed delivers event E101 twice, followed by E102. The strategy intends one rebalance per completed event, so the expected count is two distinct intents. If each delivery creates a fresh random order ID, the bot can accidentally produce three orders. A deterministic intent key such as strategy-version plus symbol plus decision timestamp ties retries to the same decision.

Now crash after a broker accepts E101's order but before acknowledgement is stored. Local absence of confirmation means unknown external state, not rejection. Reconcile using the stable client identifier and broker records before deciding whether another submission is permissible. Identifier support and retry semantics are adapter-specific; verify the actual broker contract.

## Make replay a first-class tool

Keep an immutable input log and enough state to reconstruct what each component believed. Test duplicate events, a missing sequence number, late data, an out-of-order acknowledgement, and a fill arriving during cancellation. Record the transition and the reason for every rejected action.

A single owner of account mutations makes reasoning easier. If multiple workers are introduced, use a durable transactional boundary and uniqueness constraints. An in-memory set alone does not survive a crash or coordinate two processes.

assignment.solution: Preserve the intent and stable client ID, query the external order and fill records, then reconcile before retrying. Durable uniqueness must survive restart and coordinate writers; the small loop demonstrates only the counting rule.

## A timestamp is part of the value

A price needs an instrument, venue or source, currency, event timestamp, receipt timestamp, and adjustment convention. A financial statement also needs its publication timestamp and revision identity. Calendar dates alone are insufficient when a decision depends on intraday availability.

Store a consistent clock representation and convert to the exchange's session schedule at the boundary. Daylight-saving changes, holidays, half-days, and trading halts should come from a maintained calendar or broker session interface. Never equate a weekday with an open market. The offline project uses a supplied session-open flag rather than pretending to implement an exchange calendar.

Distinguish a missing bar from a genuine zero return. Mixing adjusted historical closes with raw order prices can fabricate a signal around splits. Keep corporate actions and total-return assumptions separate from executable quotes.

$$
\text{Age}=t_{decision}-t_{event};\quad 0\leq\text{Age}\leq\text{limit}
$$

## A worked example

A quote event is timestamped 10:00:00.000 and arrives at 10:00:00.400. At a decision time of 10:00:00.900, its age from the event clock is 900 ms. Under a stipulated 750 ms freshness limit, the bot rejects a new entry even though network transport took only 400 ms.

A second quote carries a timestamp after the decision time because of clock skew. It must not pass merely because the computed age is negative. Validate both clock ordering and a maximum age. These thresholds are policy examples, not universal trading standards.

## Reconstruct the information set

For each decision, retain the exact quote or bar ID and the latest eligible filing version. A March release describing December cannot enter a February historical decision. Reject unsupported instruments and nonfinite or nonpositive prices before computing exposure.

The assignment should include fixtures for stale data, future timestamps, duplicate bars, missing volume, a split, and a closed session. Explain whether each causes an abstention, a delayed decision, or a research-only adjustment. Avoid filling a data gap with generated prices while labeling the result historical.

modules.title: Feature engineering and reproducible signals
modules.subtitle: Build past-only features with explicit warm-up, scale, and version rules shared by research and execution.
modules.objective: Build past-only features with explicit warm-up, scale, and version rules shared by research and execution.
modules.reading: Deliverable: a feature dictionary and exact input/output fixtures. Read the preprocessing consistency reference linked from the course plan.
modules.content:
## Treat features as versioned computations

Define each feature with its input field, window, lag, adjustment basis, missing-data rule, and units. A twenty-bar return and a twenty-calendar-day return need not be identical. A trailing average that includes the current completed bar is available only after that bar completes.

Warm-up is a state, not a zero. If a feature needs twenty valid observations and only twelve exist, the model should see an unavailable input or abstain under a documented rule. Filling the missing feature with zero can change a model's meaning and create unexpected orders.

Use the same transformations in training and inference. Fitted preprocessing belongs to the training artifact, while rolling calculations require a defined historical window. A price-level feature can drift with splits or nominal scale; return, ratio, or normalized features can be more interpretable but do not automatically become stationary.

$$
Momentum_t=P_t/P_{t-L}-1
$$

## A worked example

Completed closes are 100, 102, 101, and 104. A three-period simple return at the final close is 104/100 − 1 = 4%. The three most recent completed closes average (102 + 101 + 104)/3 = 102.333. The final close is about 1.63% above that average.

This is a feature calculation, not proof of trend profitability. If the decision instead occurs before the final close, 104 is unavailable and both inputs must be recomputed from earlier data. Feature timing determines the earliest possible execution.

## A reproducibility check

Save a tiny input fixture and expected feature values. Compare research and running-bot outputs on identical data, including a missing observation and the first eligible warm-up point. Record model and feature versions together so an old model cannot silently consume a reordered feature vector.

When a new feature is proposed, document the economic hypothesis before tuning its window. Log rejected variants and retain a baseline. A precise calculation can still be an overfit research choice.

modules.title: Rule-based strategy bots
modules.subtitle: Convert a signal into a target position and reconcile that target with holdings and outstanding orders.
modules.objective: Convert a signal into a target position and reconcile that target with holdings and outstanding orders.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Separate the desired end state from the instruction sent now. A binary signal can mean a target weight of 0% or 10%; it does not mean buy another 10% on every iteration. Convert weight to shares using a dated equity estimate and an executable price convention. Specify rounding, minimum lot size, cash reserves, and when a target expires.

Outstanding orders are commitments. A pending buy contributes positive shares and a pending sell contributes negative shares to the projected holding. Ignoring them causes repeated rebalancing to overshoot. A cancellation request does not remove that commitment until its result is known.

$$
q_{new}=q_{target}-q_{held}-q_{pending,buy}+q_{pending,sell}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor targets 200 shares and holds 120. With no open orders the buy requirement is 80 shares. With a previously accepted buy of 50 shares still outstanding, the residual is only 30. If 20 of that order fill, holdings become 140 and remaining commitments become 30; the residual stays 30. This invariance is a useful test of the accounting.

If the signal disappears, first reconcile or cancel the existing buy. Do not immediately submit a 120-share sell while assuming the buy vanished. Treat conflicting instructions as an order-management problem.

## Implementation and review

Implement target calculation as a pure function of a versioned snapshot. The order manager, not the signal function, owns retries. Introduce a no-trade band so negligible target changes do not create excessive turnover. Record the raw target, rounded target, existing holdings, commitments, and final permitted instruction. Compare the same rule against cash and a declared passive benchmark using identical costs and dates.

target = 200
held = 120
pending = 50
print("Residual buy shares:", target - held - pending)
print("After partial fill:", target - (held + 20) - (pending - 20))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: The residual is 30 in both states: 150−100−20 and 150−110−10. Holdings and outstanding commitments move together on a fill. The target should not be re-added on each tick.

modules.title: Trend rules, breakouts, and turnover
modules.subtitle: Specify an executable trend rule with entry, exit, warm-up, and turnover controls.
modules.objective: Specify an executable trend rule with entry, exit, warm-up, and turnover controls.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A rule must define the information window precisely. For a breakout observed at today's completed close, compare that close with an earlier high window that excludes today. Including today's high changes the question and can make a strict close-above-high test impossible. A moving-average rule instead compares levels computed from a declared window.

Use separate entry and exit thresholds when a small fluctuation would otherwise churn the portfolio. This hysteresis is a design choice with a trade-off: less turnover can delay an exit. Do not select the band after inspecting the final evaluation period.

$$
\text{Entry threshold}=\max(H_{t-L},\ldots,H_{t-1})(1+b)
$$

## A worked example

Earlier highs are 100, 102, and 101. A completed close of 103 exceeds the prior maximum of 102. Under an illustrative rule requiring a 0.5% breakout, the entry threshold is 102.51, so the signal qualifies. A 1.5% band would require 103.53 and would not qualify. Execution occurs on a later eligible event, whose price need not equal 103.

A backtest earns 1.2% gross while turning the portfolio over six one-way notional equivalents. At 15 bps per equivalent, estimated trading costs are 0.9%, leaving 0.3% before other omitted costs.

## Implementation and review

Build a fixture for a flat market, a gap, a missing close, and a split-adjustment mismatch. Evaluate a small preregistered parameter grid on training and validation windows, then freeze it. Report return, drawdown, time in market, turnover, and sensitivity to costs. A trend indicator is a descriptive transformation; the ability to compute it does not establish an economic edge.

prior_high = max([100, 102, 101])
print("Breakout threshold:", prior_high * 1.005)
print("Entry signal:", 103 > prior_high * 1.005)
print("Net percent:", 1.2 - 6 * 0.15)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Create a prior-window breakout test with earlier maximum 80, band 1%, and close 80.5. Explain which next-event execution assumption you will test.
assignment.solution: The threshold is 80.8, so no entry qualifies. A later marketable fill can gap away from the signal close; specify costs and a fresh price before sizing.

options: To reduce frequent reversals near a boundary
To eliminate the need for costs
exercises.explanation: Hysteresis can reduce churn while introducing delayed responses.

modules.title: Mean reversion and pairs hypotheses
modules.subtitle: Distinguish a normalized deviation from evidence of reversion and account for both legs of a spread.
modules.objective: Distinguish a normalized deviation from evidence of reversion and account for both legs of a spread.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A z-score describes deviation relative to an estimated mean and scale. It is not a guarantee that price will return to a historical level. Structural changes can move both the mean and variance. Specify the estimation window, fit the relationship using past data, and explain why a temporary displacement might close.

For pairs, define a spread such as A minus beta times B. Correlation of returns does not prove that this price spread is stationary. A fitted hedge ratio, a stationarity diagnostic, and an economic relationship answer different questions. Check sensitivity to sample choice and corporate changes before treating a spread as tradable.

$$
z_t=(s_t-\mu_{train})/\sigma_{train}
$$

## A worked example

A spread of 14 has a training mean of 10 and standard deviation 2, giving a z-score of 2. Harbor's paper research rule considers selling the spread above 1.5. That requires short A and long beta units of B under the stated sign convention; the current in-app long/cash sandbox cannot express both legs.

If the planned legs are $10,000 long and $10,000 short, net dollar exposure is zero but gross exposure is $20,000. Fees, stock borrow, asymmetric fills, beta mismatch, and abrupt divergence can still produce a loss.

## Implementation and review

Keep pairs work as a research worksheet unless the execution engine explicitly supports borrow availability, short margin, and two-leg state. Test a one-leg fill, a borrow recall, and a spread that never reverts. Define an exit based on elapsed time or invalidated evidence as well as the signal. Zero estimated net exposure must never bypass gross and concentration limits.

print("Spread z-score:", (spread - 10) / 2)
print("Gross exposure:", abs(10000) + abs(-10000))
print("Net exposure:", 10000 - 10000)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: z is −2. A proposed long-spread trade can continue falling and either leg may fill alone. Gross exposure, borrow, margin, and hedge error remain material.

modules.subtitle: Evaluate a frozen trading rule using a declared information cutoff, execution delay, benchmark, and cost model.
modules.objective: Evaluate a frozen trading rule using a declared information cutoff, execution delay, benchmark, and cost model.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Separate signal time, order time, and fill time. A strategy computed from a completed closing bar cannot assume it entered earlier at that bar's open. An OHLC bar also does not reveal whether its high preceded its low. Any intrabar stop or limit convention is an assumption that needs documentation.

Keep research selection distinct from final evaluation. Changing a window after seeing the holdout makes that period part of development. Record every tried variant, fit preprocessing on training data, and keep an untouched later segment for the final frozen rule. Corporate actions, delistings, and availability timestamps belong in the data audit.

$$
\Pi=q(P_{exit}-P_{entry})-f q(P_{entry}+P_{exit})
$$

## A worked example

Harbor signals at a close of 100 and buys 10 shares at the next open of 102. Later it sells at 104. At 5 bps commission on each notional, entry commission is $0.51 and exit commission $0.52. Net P&L is $18.97. Pretending entry occurred at the signal close would overstate the gross profit by $20.

If slippage is modeled in the fill price, do not subtract the same slippage again as a separate ledger fee. Compare with a passive position using the same timestamps, capital, and cost convention.

## Implementation and review

Review an order-by-order trace in addition to aggregate statistics. Report drawdown, turnover, exposure, number of independent decisions, and a cost stress. A smooth curve from few trades does not support a precise Sharpe claim. Use the sandbox to demonstrate timing and costs; use the offline project for event and ledger failure tests. Neither establishes a live execution advantage.

modules.title: Quotes, spread, and implementation shortfall
modules.subtitle: Measure an execution against a declared decision benchmark while distinguishing spread, impact, and delay.
modules.objective: Measure an execution against a declared decision benchmark while distinguishing spread, impact, and delay.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A quote is an indication at a particular time, size, and venue. The midpoint is useful as a benchmark but is not necessarily executable. A marketable buy typically consumes offered liquidity; a resting limit may fail to fill or fill when the market moves against it. Better price and greater fill certainty are competing objectives.

Implementation shortfall compares execution with a decision benchmark, adjusted for trade direction. Explicit fees can be added separately. Spread, market impact, and delay are explanatory components whose estimates may overlap; avoid presenting a precise causal decomposition without the necessary data.

$$
IS_{bps}=10^4 d(P_{fill}/P_{decision}-1),\quad d\in\{+1,-1\}
$$

## A worked example

The bid is 99.90 and the ask 100.10, so the midpoint is 100 and the quoted spread is 20 bps. A buy filling at 100.12 costs 12 bps relative to that midpoint before commission. Half the quoted spread accounts for 10 bps in a simple interpretation; the extra 2 bps cannot be confidently called permanent impact from this single observation.

A sell at 99.88 also has 12 bps adverse shortfall under a direction-adjusted convention. Use consistent signs so a worse sell is not accidentally reported as a benefit.

## Implementation and review

Store the benchmark's source, timestamp, and size with each decision. Report fill rate and unfilled opportunity cost alongside the average cost of completed trades; measuring only successful fills can flatter passive strategies. Paper fills do not reproduce queue priority, hidden liquidity, or adverse selection. The course uses explicit toy assumptions that should be challenged before interpreting results.

print("Quoted spread (bps):", round((100.10 - 99.90) / mid * 10000, 2))
print("Buy shortfall (bps):", round((100.12 / mid - 1) * 10000, 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

modules.title: Order state machines and cancellation races
modules.subtitle: Handle acknowledgements, partial fills, cancellations, rejections, and ambiguous submissions without losing commitments.
modules.objective: Handle acknowledgements, partial fills, cancellations, rejections, and ambiguous submissions without losing commitments.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Model submission, acknowledgement, partial fill, complete fill, cancellation, and rejection as explicit states with legal transitions. A timeout is an observation about communication, not necessarily an order state. Broker messages can arrive twice or out of order, so deduplicate by durable identity and reconcile cumulative quantities.

Separate an intent ID from an external order ID and a fill ID. One intent may have a documented cancel-and-replace sequence, while one order may have many fills. Track original quantity, cumulative filled quantity, remaining quantity, and cancellation status. Do not assume a cancellation acknowledgement erases earlier fills.

$$
q_{remaining}=q_{original}-\sum_i q_{fill,i}
$$

## A worked example

An order buys 100 shares. Forty fill, leaving 60. The bot requests cancellation, but 15 more fill before the cancellation completes. The ledger must contain 55 bought shares; the successful cancellation removes only the remaining 45. If the 15-share fill message is replayed, holdings remain 55.

If the broker reports cumulative filled quantity of 55, do not treat it as 55 additional shares after already booking 40. Distinguish incremental fill messages from cumulative order updates in the adapter contract.

## Implementation and review

Build a transition table and test every terminal state. Preserve unknown orders as risk commitments until reconciliation resolves them. Record rejected transitions for investigation instead of forcing state to match the latest message blindly. The offline lab demonstrates partial fills and idempotent fill records; a real asynchronous adapter additionally needs broker-specific cancel races and sequencing behavior.

print("Canceled remainder:", original - filled)

    return data["close"] < 0

modules.title: Execution schedules: TWAP, VWAP, and participation
modules.subtitle: Choose and evaluate a slicing policy with explicit urgency, liquidity, and completion constraints.
modules.objective: Choose and evaluate a slicing policy with explicit urgency, liquidity, and completion constraints.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

TWAP distributes quantity over time; VWAP schedules against an estimated volume profile; a participation policy sizes child orders relative to observed or estimated market volume. Each needs a remaining-quantity cap, eligibility rules, and an end-of-window policy. Naming the algorithm does not define its actual fill mechanics.

Fast execution reduces waiting exposure but can consume expensive liquidity. Slow execution may reduce immediate pressure while risking price movement or an unfinished parent order. Models that optimize this trade-off rely on assumptions about volatility, impact, and constraints; there is no universally optimal schedule.

$$
q_{child}\leq\min(q_{remaining},\rho V_{eligible})
$$

## A worked example

A 1,000-share parent has four equal time buckets. TWAP requests 250 per bucket. A forecast volume profile of 10%, 20%, 40%, and 30% suggests VWAP child targets of 100, 200, 400, and 300. Under a 5% participation cap, a bucket with 4,000 shares of eligible volume permits at most 200 shares, even when the schedule asks for 400.

The remaining 200 cannot simply disappear from the report. The parent needs a documented carry-forward, cancellation, or urgency change, with risk approval. Do not use a bucket's eventual full volume for an order placed before that volume was known.

## Implementation and review

Simulate sparse volume, a missed bucket, a session ending early, and a late cancellation. Report both shortfall and completion percentage. A schedule should preserve parent quantity after partial fills and retries. Cap each child by remaining authorized quantity as well as participation; otherwise a catch-up rule can overfill the original decision.
