The default paper replay reconciles to $10,025.39 equity, three fills, $0.61 fees, and an active halt. The artificial ridge comparison yields MSE about 0.495983 versus 30.5 for its baseline. The evidence validator accepts the supported 120-million revenue record and derives 20% growth. Each result answers a different acceptance question.

Suppose an altered implementation reports the same final equity but creates two fills for E1 and later offsets them. The final number matches while event idempotency fails. Review both state invariants and the full transition trace; a favorable final balance cannot excuse invalid intermediate actions.

Use a 100-point self-assessment: decision and data contract 15, execution and ledger evidence 25, risk and restart behavior 20, ML evaluation 15, AI evidence and permissions 15, and incident/release documentation 10. Require at least 80 points and no unresolved failure of cash/share conservation, duplicate handling, persistent halts, or source validation. modules.title: Bytes, encodings, and cryptographic hashes
modules.subtitle: Distinguish byte representation, hashing, and encryption, and identify the exact data committed by a digest.
modules.objective: Distinguish byte representation, hashing, and encryption, and identify the exact data committed by a digest.
modules.reading: Unit 1 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A protocol operates on bytes. UTF-8 text, hexadecimal display, and an integer's binary encoding can represent related ideas while producing different byte sequences. A hash commits to the bytes actually supplied; it does not interpret a business meaning or normalize a document automatically. Define field ordering, lengths, encodings, and domain tags before signing or hashing structured data.

A cryptographic digest is deterministic and fixed length. Preimage resistance concerns finding an input for a specified digest; collision resistance concerns finding any two different inputs with the same digest. Neither property makes hashing encryption, authenticates the sender, or establishes that an input claim is true.

$$
N=2^b,\quad collision\ scale\approx\sqrt N
$$

## A worked example

A toy 16-bit digest has 65,536 possible outputs. Generic collision search reaches the birthday scale around 256 samples, while a specified target requires a different search problem. These are order-of-magnitude illustrations, not security guarantees for a real truncated scheme.

The downloadable Node lab computes SHA-256 with the standard library and tests the known digest of the three UTF-8 bytes abc. Adding a newline changes the input. The guided Python worksheet below illustrates the combinatorics; actual hashing runs in the downloaded project.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write a serialization specification before building the ledger. The lab uses fixed ordered tuples and distinct payment, block, leaf, and branch domains. Reproduce the standard hash vector, compare a one-byte change, and record both input bytes and algorithm name. Do not design a new hash function for this project. A digest can demonstrate that an artifact matches a prior commitment only when the reference commitment and its provenance are also trustworthy.
modules.code:
import math
print("Toy digest space:", 2 ** 16)
print("Birthday scale:", math.sqrt(2 ** 16))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Run the native-chain hash test. Compare UTF-8 abc and abc followed by a newline. Explain why identical human meaning need not imply identical digests.
assignment.solution: The inputs contain different bytes, so the digests differ. Hashing commits to an agreed encoding; it does not perform semantic normalization or prove authorship.

modules.title: Merkle commitments and inclusion proofs
modules.subtitle: Construct a transaction commitment and verify an ordered inclusion path without confusing inclusion with transaction validity.
modules.objective: Construct a transaction commitment and verify an ordered inclusion path without confusing inclusion with transaction validity.
modules.reading: Unit 1 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A Merkle tree combines leaf hashes into parent hashes until one root commits to the collection. A proof supplies sibling hashes along one path. Verification recomputes the root in the specified left/right order. The protocol must define leaf encoding, branch encoding, ordering, treatment of odd counts, and empty-tree behavior.

The local project prefixes leaves and branches with different bytes and duplicates the last node at an odd level. Its block header also commits to the transaction count, since duplicate-last constructions require care when interpreting collection length. This is an educational commitment format, not Ethereum's execution-state trie or Bitcoin's exact wire protocol.

$$
proof\ depth=\log_2 n\quad(n\text{ a power of two})
$$

## A worked example

A balanced tree of eight leaves requires three sibling hashes for an inclusion path. For a five-leaf example, the lab's tests verify every path through the odd-count construction. Changing a signed transaction amount makes the original proof fail against the original root.

A valid inclusion proof only establishes membership under a root. It does not show that the root belongs to a finalized canonical block, that the signer had funds, or that all other transactions are valid. Those are separate validation and consensus questions.

## Implementation and interpretation

Trace one proof by hand using symbolic leaf labels before using actual digests. Then run the downloaded odd-leaf tests and alter a transaction and a sibling direction independently. Record which commitment changed. Keep the authoritative root and its chain context with the proof; accepting an arbitrary root supplied by the same untrusted party proves little about an external ledger. Explain the difference between proving one transaction's inclusion and replaying all state transitions.
modules.formula: proof\ depth=\log_2 n\quad(n\text{ a power of two})
modules.code:
import math
print("Sibling hashes for eight leaves:", math.log(8) / math.log(2))
print("Sibling hashes for sixteen leaves:", math.log(16) / math.log(2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Verify each path in the five-transaction fixture, then change one amount. Explain two additional checks needed before treating an included payment as accepted money.
assignment.solution: The changed leaf should fail against the old root. Also validate the payment and resulting balances, and establish the block's accepted chain/finality context; inclusion alone is insufficient.

modules.title: Public keys and digital signatures
modules.subtitle: Verify signed messages with established libraries and distinguish the cryptographic schemes used by different chains.
modules.objective: Verify signed messages with established libraries and distinguish the cryptographic schemes used by different chains.
modules.reading: Unit 1 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A signature lets a verifier check that a message was authorized by the holder of a corresponding private key under a specified algorithm. The private key remains secret; the public key and signature can be distributed. Verification must bind the exact intended message and application domain. A valid signature does not establish the signer's real-world identity, sufficient balance, or permission under every contract.

This lab uses Ed25519 through Node's crypto library. Ethereum externally owned accounts conventionally use secp256k1 ECDSA instead. Their key formats, signature procedures, and address derivations are different. Do not copy an address recipe between schemes or implement signing arithmetic from a short tutorial.

$$
Verify(pk,message,signature)\in\{true,false\}
$$

## A worked example

Alice signs a local payment of 20 atomic units to Bob with nonce 0. Verification succeeds for those fields. Changing the amount to 21 invalidates the signature. Substituting Bob's address as the claimed sender also fails because the lab checks the address against the supplied public key.

A signature remains cryptographically valid after its payment has been spent. The account nonce and ledger balance checks provide replay and spending rules; signature verification alone cannot replace them.

## Implementation and interpretation

Generate ephemeral keys using the platform's cryptographic generator. Keep private keys out of logs, browser bundles, and project submissions. The downloadable tests exercise valid signatures, changed amounts, sender substitution, and a wrong network domain. Submit public identifiers and test outcomes only. Explain why the project's SHA-256 hash of an encoded Ed25519 public key is a local address convention and cannot receive assets on Ethereum or Bitcoin.

print("Signed amount:", 20)
print("Tampered amount:", 21)
print("Amount change:", 21 - 20)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Run the signature tests and document the fields bound by the message. Explain why a replayed valid signature still needs ledger rejection.
assignment.solution: The signed tuple binds domain, network, sender, recipient, amount, nonce, and public key. Replaying it preserves signature validity but violates the already consumed account nonce.

modules.title: Wallets, replay domains, and transaction nonces
modules.subtitle: Treat a wallet as a signing and state-coordination interface, with explicit separation between secrets, network identity, and sequence numbers.
modules.objective: Treat a wallet as a signing and state-coordination interface, with explicit separation between secrets, network identity, and sequence numbers.
modules.reading: Unit 1 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A wallet manages keys or access to a signer and helps construct transactions. Assets are represented by ledger state, not stored inside the application icon. Recovery therefore concerns the signing authority and its supported derivation or backup scheme, while account history must be read from the intended chain. Seed phrases are secrets and should never be entered into this course.

A transaction nonce is an account sequence number in this model. It is distinct from the nonce searched during proof of work and from cryptographic ephemeral values inside some signature algorithms. Reusing the word does not make these mechanisms interchangeable. A network/domain identifier further prevents a locally valid message from being accepted in another protocol context.

$$
nonce_{accepted}=nonce_{expected},\quad nonce_{next}=nonce_{expected}+1
$$

## A worked example

If Alice's next expected payment nonce is 3, a signed payment with nonce 2 is a replay and nonce 4 is premature under this strict sequential ledger. Exactly nonce 3 can proceed to the balance check. After an accepted payment, the next expected value is 4.

Two concurrent wallet tasks that both read nonce 3 can create conflicting intentions. A real wallet or transaction service needs coordination and reconciliation with accepted chain state. Increasing the number locally without tracking submitted outcomes can leave a gap.

## Implementation and interpretation

Draw a wallet flow from recipient review through message construction, signing, submission, pending state, and accepted-state reconciliation. The local lab has no mempool or replacement policy, so it rejects out-of-sequence payments rather than simulating those features. Test stale and future nonces, wrong domains, and recovery by replaying accepted blocks. Never infer finality from a wallet's submitted label alone. Keep signing permission distinct from unlimited token allowances granted to another contract.

modules.title: Native coins, tokens, and ledger models
modules.subtitle: Choose whether an asset belongs to a base protocol or a smart contract and specify its accounting representation.
modules.objective: Choose whether an asset belongs to a base protocol or a smart contract and specify its accounting representation.
modules.reading: Unit 2 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A native coin is accounted for by a blockchain's own state-transition rules. A token on an existing chain is accounted for by a contract within that chain. Deploying an ERC-20 contract creates a token ledger; it does not create a new consensus network or replace the host chain's native gas asset. The course builds one example of each locally.

An account model tracks balances and sequence numbers. A UTXO model tracks unspent outputs consumed and created by transactions. Both need authorization and conservation rules, but their data structures and replay handling differ. The native lab uses accounts for clarity and does not claim to implement Bitcoin's UTXO or Ethereum's full execution model.

$$
S_{next}=S_{current}+authorized\ issuance-burns
$$

## A worked example

The native project begins with 1,000 atomic units assigned in genesis. Alice sends 100 to Bob and the first block issues a 10-unit reward to Alice. Her balance becomes 910, Bob's becomes 100, and total supply is 1,010. The transfer moves existing units; the authorized reward increases supply.

The ERC-20 project instead creates one million whole CEDAR tokens in a constructor on an in-process EVM. Token balances are separate from the local native test currency used to execute the deployment.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write an asset specification covering ledger type, unit scale, initial allocation, supply changes, signing rules, and host-chain dependence. Identify the code path allowed to create new units. Compare a transfer with a mint and with a transaction fee. A name and ticker do not make two assets identical: an ERC-20 identity requires its chain and contract address, while the native lab is identified by its own genesis and network rules.

modules.title: Consensus, proof of work, and finality
modules.subtitle: Separate valid state transitions from agreement on chain history and understand the limits of a single-process mining demonstration.
modules.objective: Separate valid state transitions from agreement on chain history and understand the limits of a single-process mining demonstration.
modules.reading: Unit 2 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Validation asks whether a proposed block obeys protocol rules. Consensus also addresses which valid history participants accept when competing histories exist. Proof of work attaches a computational cost to candidate blocks; proof of stake uses a different validator and incentive structure. The specific fork-choice and finality rules belong to each protocol and cannot be inferred from a generic blockchain diagram.

The downloaded native chain deliberately omits peers, network delay, fork choice, difficulty adjustment, and economic security. It checks a trivial hash target and extends one current tip. This demonstrates commitment and validation mechanics but cannot establish distributed agreement or protect a public currency.

$$
p=2^{-12},\quad E[trials]=1/p=4096
$$

## A worked example

The toy target requires three leading hexadecimal zero characters, equivalent to 12 zero bits. For a uniformly distributed digest, success probability per trial is 1/4,096 and expected trials are 4,096. Actual attempts vary randomly; a successful block may arrive much sooner or later.

A valid proof of work cannot authorize overspending. The validator still rejects a block containing an invalid signature, nonce, reward, or balance transition, even when its hash meets the target.

## Implementation and interpretation

Run a local block and inspect its hash and header fields. Explain why changing the parent or Merkle root invalidates the old hash. Then use the supplied tests to show a valid-looking work header cannot bypass the reward rule. In a design memo, list what a multi-node system would additionally need: peer communication, chain selection, finality interpretation, synchronization, adversarial resource limits, and recovery. Do not label the successful local demonstration as a secure public network.

print("Expected hash trials:", 2 ** 12)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: Its computational cost is intentionally tiny and there are no adversarial peers. Fork choice, synchronization, distributed finality, and economic/resource assumptions are omitted.

modules.title: Atomic transaction and block validation
modules.subtitle: Validate signatures, nonces, commitments, and conservation before accepting any state changes from a candidate block.
modules.objective: Validate signatures, nonces, commitments, and conservation before accepting any state changes from a candidate block.
modules.reading: Unit 2 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A validator must reject an entire invalid block without leaving partial economic effects behind. Checking a signature is only one step. The local lab verifies the network domain, next height, parent hash, transaction commitment, proof-of-work target, permitted reward, integer amounts, sender identity, sequential nonce, and available balance.

It applies transactions to copied maps. Only after every transaction and the supply invariant pass does it replace accepted state. This makes a late failure atomic. A mutable reference to accepted balances or block history would undermine that guarantee, so the lab also returns copies from its inspection methods.

$$
\sum_a balance_a=S,\quad invalid\ block\Rightarrow state'=state
$$

## A worked example

Alice has 910 units after the first block. A candidate second block includes a valid 50-unit payment followed by an unaffordable 1,000-unit payment. The candidate fails. Alice remains at 910, Bob remains at 100, and no second block reward is issued. Applying the first transaction permanently before checking the second would corrupt state.

A self-transfer subtracts then adds to the same account and must conserve balance while consuming one nonce. The tests cover this edge case because simplistic updates can accidentally mint or destroy units.

## Implementation and interpretation

Order checks so malformed data fails clearly before expensive or stateful operations. Preserve the exact accepted snapshot before each adverse test and compare it afterward. Test duplicate payments, future nonces, a forged reward, altered transaction bytes, and mutation of returned snapshots. Replay all accepted blocks into a new instance with the same genesis and compare the resulting state. Agreement with a fresh replay is a useful accounting check, though it does not substitute for distributed consensus.

print("Supply after rejected second block:", 1010)
print("Self-transfer net change:", -50 + 50)

    return data["close"] < 0

## Model and assumptions

Download the coin-lab archive and run node native-chain.mjs with Node 22 or later. This component needs no installed packages. It generates ephemeral Ed25519 keys, defines genesis allocation, signs a payment, constructs a Merkle commitment, searches a small proof-of-work target, validates the block, and prints public results. It opens no network port and connects to no chain.

The native coin has integer atomic units, an initial supply of 1,000, a reward of ten per accepted block, and a cap of 1,100. The reward becomes available after the block's transactions validate. These are original teaching rules chosen for transparent arithmetic, not an economic recommendation.

$$
S_h=1000+\min(10h,100)
$$

## A worked example

The default run pays 100 units from Alice to Bob and rewards Alice ten. Expected output includes signatureValid=true, proofValid=true, aliceBalance=910, bobBalance=100, supply=1010, and height=1. Public addresses and the mined hash vary because keys are freshly generated.

A second payment of 25 from Bob back to Alice, with another ten-unit reward to Alice, yields balances 945 and 75 and supply 1,020. The tests reconstruct the same state through independent replay.

## Implementation and interpretation

Run node --test native-chain.test.mjs and retain its results. Add an altered-amount case, a duplicate nonce, and a block that fails after an earlier valid transaction. Record the unchanged accepted state after each rejection. Describe the omitted peer network, persistence, fee market, fork choice, and production key custody. Your deliverable is a reproducible educational coin implementation and its validation evidence, not a claim that a public cryptocurrency has launched.

modules.title: EVM execution, gas, and integer token units
modules.subtitle: Trace contract execution costs and represent token amounts without floating-point rounding.
modules.objective: Trace contract execution costs and represent token amounts without floating-point rounding.
modules.reading: Unit 3 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

The EVM executes contract instructions under a gas budget. Gas measures execution work; its monetary cost depends on the transaction's effective gas price. A transaction that reverts does not preserve its attempted contract state changes, but an included failed transaction can still consume gas. An off-chain read and an on-chain state-changing transaction have different execution contexts.

ERC-20 balances are integers in atomic units. Decimals provide a display scale; they do not make Solidity balances floating-point values. The local contract uses 18 decimals. Its tests use JavaScript BigInt and ethers parseUnits to preserve exact amounts rather than converting large token balances through Number.

$$
atomic=display\times10^{decimals},\quad fee=gasUsed\times effectiveGasPrice
$$

## A worked example

A display amount 1.25 with six decimals corresponds to 1,250,000 atomic units. With 18 decimals the scale is much larger, but the rule is the same. A transaction using a stipulated 50,000 gas at an effective price of 20 gwei costs 1,000,000 gwei, or .001 native ether units. This arithmetic is a fixture, not a current fee quote.

The project's compiler explicitly targets the Shanghai EVM implemented by the local test provider. Compiler version and EVM target are separate build settings and must agree with the execution environment.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write amount conversion tests for whole, fractional, zero, and excessively precise inputs. Record compiler, optimization settings, and EVM target with deployed bytecode. Explain why an ERC-20 balance cannot pay native gas unless an additional supported mechanism explicitly provides that service. Keep estimated gas separate from actual receipt gas, and do not interpret a successful estimate as a guarantee that later execution succeeds.

print("Illustrative native fee:", 50000 * 20 / 10 ** 9)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: The amount is 250,000,000 atomic units and the fee is .0012 native ether units. Decimal string parsing and integer arithmetic avoid rounding large or fractional token amounts.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

The CedarCoin source imports the pinned OpenZeppelin ERC20 implementation and adds a constructor that creates one million whole tokens for a chosen recipient. The wrapper has no owner role, external mint function, transfer tax, blacklist, proxy, or upgrade entry point. That small scope makes the intended authority easy to inspect.

An ERC-20 interface standardizes balances, transfers, allowances, and events. It does not by itself promise demand, redeemability, legal rights, or a fixed supply. Those properties come from the actual contract and surrounding arrangements. Read inherited code and dependencies when reviewing an implementation, rather than treating the wrapper's short length as its complete behavior.

$$
S_0=1{,}000{,}000\times10^{18}\;atomic\ units
$$

## A worked example

At deployment, totalSupply is 1,000,000×10^18 atomic units and the designated recipient owns that amount. A transfer of 100 whole tokens leaves 999,900 with the original recipient and 100 with the receiver. Total supply remains one million.

The constructor calls an internal mint operation, but no public function exposes that operation afterward. The test also inspects the ABI for the absent mint and upgrade names; this supports this particular wrapper's stated design, not a universal proof about every similarly named token.

## Implementation and interpretation

Read CedarCoin.sol alongside the dependency documentation. Identify the constructor argument, display metadata, scale, supply expression, and inherited transfer methods. Compile using the locked dependency tree and record the artifact hash. Modify a copy's initial supply only after updating the specification and expected tests. Keep the teaching name and project identity clear; deploying a contract with a familiar ticker does not make it another issuer's asset.

## Model and assumptions

After downloading and extracting the project, run npm ci and npm test. The token test compiles the contract with pinned solc and OpenZeppelin versions, creates an in-process Ganache EVM, deploys through ethers, and exercises the resulting contract. The process uses generated local accounts and closes its provider when finished. There is no external RPC argument or public deployment step.

A transfer moves the caller's own tokens. An allowance authorizes a named spender to transfer a bounded amount from another account. Approving an allowance does not move tokens immediately. Interfaces should make spender identity and amount clear; an allowance is a meaningful authority grant even when the transaction itself transfers nothing.

$$
allowance_{after}=allowance_{before}-authorized\ spend
$$

## A worked example

The fixture sends 100 tokens to a recipient, approves a spender for 25, and lets that spender transfer another ten to the recipient. The recipient then holds 110 and the remaining finite allowance is 15. Trying to transfer 16 through that allowance must fail without changing token balances or allowance.

The test also rejects overspending and a zero-address recipient, checks zero-value transfer events, executes twelve small transfers while reconciling supply, and compares deployed runtime bytes with the compiled artifact.

## Implementation and interpretation

Retain the compiler version, source hash, runtime hash, and passing output. Explain each assertion using the state before and after its transaction. Add an allowance revocation case in a local copy, then show that the spender cannot use the revoked amount. Do not submit account secrets. Passing these fixtures demonstrates the specified local behaviors; it does not establish that arbitrary extensions, bridges, or exchange integrations are correct.

modules.title: Minting authority, burns, vesting, and upgrades
modules.subtitle: Evaluate additional token powers as explicit design changes with separate invariants and review requirements.
modules.objective: Evaluate additional token powers as explicit design changes with separate invariants and review requirements.
modules.reading: Unit 3 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A token's economic policy is constrained by reachable code and control over that code. A mint role can expand supply, a burn function can reduce it, and an upgrade mechanism can change future behavior. A cap is only as durable as the authority able to bypass or replace its enforcement. Map every privileged action to its controller, delay, limits, and recovery procedure.

The supplied CedarCoin intentionally does not implement these extensions. This lesson asks you to design and review them on paper before adding them to a local fork. A multisignature or timelock changes the control process; it does not prove that a proposed action is sound or that signers cannot collude.

$$
mint\ capacity=cap-current\ supply
$$

## A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical token has supply 800,000 and an enforced cap of one million. A 150,000-unit mint fits the remaining 200,000 capacity, while a 250,000-unit mint does not. Burning 20,000 afterward reduces outstanding supply to 930,000 under that design. Whether burned units can later be reissued must be explicitly specified.

A two-of-three administrator setup requires two approvals, but the independence of those three controllers matters. Three keys held by one person do not provide three independent decision makers.

## Implementation and interpretation

Create an authority matrix for mint, burn, pause, vest, upgrade, and emergency recovery. State which powers are absent in the supplied contract. For each proposed extension, write invariants and boundary tests: unauthorized caller, exact cap, one unit above cap, expired or premature release, and failed external interaction. Keep immutable-source claims separate from proxy-based systems whose implementation can change. Review source and dependency changes as part of the same artifact release.

modules.title: Tokenomics and monetary dilution
modules.subtitle: Separate unit rewards, ownership dilution, purchasing power, and the source of a token's economic demand.
modules.objective: Separate unit rewards, ownership dilution, purchasing power, and the source of a token's economic demand.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Tokenomics describes issuance, distribution, use, incentives, and claims on resources. A quoted staking yield can increase a holder's units while total supply also expands. That unit reward is different from a dollar return, and a dilution-adjusted ownership calculation is different from a purchasing-power forecast. Identify who pays each reward and whether it comes from fees, new issuance, or a temporary subsidy.

Scarcity alone does not create demand. A fixed cap specifies one supply rule, while utility, redemption rights, competition, governance, and market access influence what participants are willing to exchange for units. The local teaching coins have no promised market value or redemption service.

$$
share\ growth=\frac{1+r_{units}}{1+g_{supply}}-1
$$

## A worked example

If a holder's units rise 8% while total supply rises 6%, the ratio of the holder's supply share changes by 1.08/1.06−1, approximately 1.887%. This does not guarantee a positive currency-denominated return. A price decline of 20% would make the holder's gross value factor 1.08×.8=.864, or a 13.6% loss before costs.

A reward funded by new issuance transfers relative ownership differently from a fee funded by external users. Analyze both the numerator and the system-wide denominator.

## Implementation and interpretation

Build a supply table with opening units, issuance, burns, circulating definitions, allocations, and ending units. Separate contractual rules from discretionary policy and distinguish circulating supply from total outstanding or maximum supply. In the assignment, calculate both ownership-share change and value change under an explicit price scenario. Document uncertainties in each input instead of presenting a single yield as a comprehensive investment outcome.

modules.title: Distribution schedules, vesting, and treasury accounting
modules.subtitle: Model who can access token supply over time and distinguish scheduled availability from actual market selling.
modules.objective: Model who can access token supply over time and distinguish scheduled availability from actual market selling.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An allocation table records intended ownership, while a vesting schedule specifies when units become claimable. Circulating-supply estimates depend on a declared definition of accessible holdings, locked balances, treasury units, and contractual restrictions. A date in a presentation does not enforce a lock; identify the actual custody or contract mechanism.

Unlocks can change the amount available for sale, but an unlock is not itself a market sale. Price impact depends on holder behavior, liquidity, demand, and other events. Keep the deterministic schedule calculation separate from a speculative market-response model.

$$
claimable=vested\ cumulative-already\ claimed
$$

## A worked example

A hypothetical team allocation is 120,000 units, with a 12-month cliff followed by 24 equal monthly releases. Under a rule with zero release at the cliff and the first release one month later, each release is 5,000. Six completed release dates make 30,000 cumulatively claimable. A different rule that releases an accrued amount at the cliff gives a different result and must be specified.

If 20,000 have already been claimed, the remaining claimable amount is 10,000. Claimable, claimed, and sold are three different quantities.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write boundary cases for immediately before the cliff, exactly at it, the first release, a partial claim, and the final release. Define integer rounding so total released units never exceed allocation and the final residual is handled explicitly. Reconcile treasury opening balance, incoming fees or allocations, spending, and closing balance. Do not combine token-denominated treasury gains with fiat spending power without a dated valuation convention. The supplied fixed-supply token has no vesting mechanism; this schedule is a design exercise for a separate local extension.

modules.title: AMMs & impermanent loss
modules.subtitle: Calculate a constant-product swap and distinguish fee income, slippage, and divergence from holding the original assets.
modules.objective: Calculate a constant-product swap and distinguish fee income, slippage, and divergence from holding the original assets.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A constant-product market maker relates two reserves through a curve. The marginal price at a point differs from the average price paid for a finite trade. A large trade relative to reserves moves farther along the curve and creates more price impact. Fees and implementation details modify the actual transfer calculation, so declare whether a worksheet omits them.

A liquidity provider owns a changing composition of pool reserves. After external prices move and arbitrage adjusts the pool, the value can differ from simply holding the original assets. The common impermanent-loss formula is a comparison under specific constant-product, balanced-deposit, no-fee assumptions; it is not a universal loss bound.

$$
xy=k,\quad IL(r)=\frac{2\sqrt r}{1+r}-1
$$

## A worked example

With reserves x=100 and y=10,000, the no-fee product is one million. Adding ten units of x leaves y=1,000,000/110≈9,090.909, so the trader receives about 909.091 y. Average received price is 90.909 y per x, below the initial marginal ratio 100.

For a fourfold relative price move under the standard no-fee comparison, 2√4/(1+4)−1=−20%. Fee revenue could offset some divergence, while adverse conditions can introduce additional risks not included in this expression.

## Implementation and interpretation

Reproduce reserve conservation and compare several trade sizes. Separate quoted output, a minimum-output limit, actual execution, and total transaction cost. For a liquidity position, report both its absolute value change and its performance relative to holding. The local ERC-20 project does not deploy a pool; this lesson is a reserve and risk worksheet, not a claim that creating a token also creates usable market liquidity.

modules.title: Crypto arbitrage and imperfect neutrality
modules.subtitle: Reconcile the legs, funding, custody, and timing of a nominally hedged crypto position.
modules.objective: Reconcile the legs, funding, custody, and timing of a nominally hedged crypto position.
modules.reading: Unit 4 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An arbitrage description often compares two quoted prices while ignoring whether both legs can execute and remain funded. Cross-venue trading introduces settlement delay, custody, withdrawal restrictions, and asynchronous fills. A spot-versus-derivative position may offset first-order directional exposure while retaining basis, funding, liquidation, and counterparty risk.

Neutrality depends on the instruments' payoff units and current sensitivities. Equal displayed quantities do not necessarily create equal dollar delta, especially with inverse contracts, options, or changing collateral value. Specify the actual instruments and sizing convention before describing a hedge as neutral.

$$
\pi=(S_T-S_0)+(F_0-F_T)-costs
$$

## A worked example

A simplified position buys one unit of spot at 100 and shorts one linear futures unit at 103. If both settle at 101 with no costs, spot gains one and the short gains two, totaling three. If combined fees and financing are 1.2, the stipulated net gain is 1.8.

If only the spot leg fills and the price falls to 95, the account has a five-unit loss and no executed futures hedge. The intended spread trade did not remove the actual directional exposure.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write a leg-by-leg ledger including cash, collateral, contract multiplier, fees, funding, and accepted fills. Stress a failed short, a collateral haircut, a delayed withdrawal, and basis widening before convergence. Avoid treating funding receipts as fixed positive income: the sign and rate can change under the stated contract. The course projects use no live exchanges, so this worksheet illustrates accounting and failure analysis rather than executing a public arbitrage strategy.

modules.title: Transaction lifecycle, gas limits, and ordering risk
modules.subtitle: Track a submitted transaction through execution and acceptance while bounding fees and swap outcomes.
modules.objective: Track a submitted transaction through execution and acceptance while bounding fees and swap outcomes.
modules.reading: Unit 5 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Submission is an intention to enter a chain's processing pipeline. A transaction can remain pending, fail, be replaced under a provider or protocol policy, or appear in a block whose acceptance later changes. Account nonces coordinate ordering; a transaction hash is an identifier, not proof that the intended state change succeeded. Inspect execution status and the accepted chain context.

A swap's minimum-output bound and deadline constrain its acceptable outcome, while gas and fee settings bound different aspects of execution. A larger priority fee can influence inclusion incentives but does not guarantee immediate inclusion or a favorable transaction order. Publicly visible intentions can also expose users to adverse ordering and sandwich-style execution risk.

$$
minimumOutput=quotedOutput(1-tolerance)
$$

## A worked example

A quote is 1,000 output units and a user permits at most 2% output shortfall, giving a minimum of 980 under this simple convention. An eventual output of 975 should fail the bound. This protects that outcome condition but does not recover every gas cost or eliminate all ordering risk.

A stipulated 100,000 gas limit at a maximum effective price of 30 gwei corresponds to .003 native units of that budget calculation. Actual charged gas and price must be read from execution evidence.

## Implementation and interpretation

Build a transaction state table with intent ID, nonce, hash, submission time, receipt status, block reference, and acceptance policy. Reconcile replacements against the same account nonce and avoid recording two intended alternatives as two accepted payments. The local native lab has strict sequential acceptance and no mempool, so document that these production lifecycle concepts are beyond its implementation. In the local EVM project, distinguish rejected estimation from an included reverted transaction when interpreting a test failure.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A contract can enforce deterministic rules over its inputs while still receiving misleading inputs. An oracle introduces a mechanism for obtaining observations such as prices; a bridge introduces assumptions about another chain's state and a process for representing or releasing assets. Trace the data and authority that cross each boundary. On-chain storage does not make an external claim automatically accurate.

External calls can transfer execution control. Checks, state updates, and interactions must be designed together, including failure behavior and reentrancy risks. The supplied CedarCoin has no oracle, bridge, or arbitrary external-call feature. Adding one changes the system being reviewed and requires its own tests and authority model.

$$
collateralValue=quantity\times acceptedPrice
$$

## A worked example

A lending rule uses collateral quantity ten and a price input of 100, producing collateral value 1,000. If the economically relevant price is actually 70, the same quantity is worth 700. Perfect integer arithmetic cannot repair the stale or manipulated input.

A bridge representation of 100 units also requires a rule connecting issued claims to valid locked or burned assets elsewhere. A ledger showing 100 claims does not prove that the backing remains available or redeemable.

## Implementation and interpretation

Draw a trust-boundary diagram with source, update frequency, freshness limits, validation rules, privileged keys, and emergency behavior. Add a stale-price case, conflicting sources, failed external call, and revoked controller. Explain what the application can verify locally and which claim depends on external participants. Avoid describing a dependency as trustless merely because it exposes a smart-contract address; inspect its validation and control mechanism. Keep a rejected external observation from silently becoming a zero price or an unrestricted mint.

modules.objective: Calculate a simplified collateral health measure and challenge liquidity, pricing, and execution assumptions together.
modules.reading: Unit 5 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A collateral health measure compares a protocol-defined portion of collateral value with debt. The exact formula, eligible assets, thresholds, oracle conventions, and liquidation process are implementation-specific. This lesson uses a simplified ratio to make the mechanics explicit, not to state a universal rule for every lending protocol.

A position can cross its liquidation threshold before a trader's preferred long-term thesis has time to recover. Price gaps, oracle delays, collateral correlation, funding changes, and liquidation execution can interact. Stress tests should recalculate the balance sheet under scenarios rather than scaling a normal-period volatility estimate and calling it complete.

$$
H=Q P\theta/D
$$

## A worked example

Collateral quantity ten at price 100 has value 1,000. With a stipulated liquidation threshold .8 and debt 600, health is 800/600≈1.333. If price falls to 70, adjusted collateral is 560 and health becomes .933. Under this fixture, a value below one makes the account potentially liquidatable.

Restoring health exactly to one at the lower price would require debt no greater than 560, so repayment of 40 reaches the boundary. A practical buffer would need a separately chosen margin and feasible funds; touching the boundary is not robust protection.

## Implementation and interpretation

Stress collateral price, debt growth, threshold changes, and available liquidation liquidity separately and jointly. Record whether the response can actually execute while the system is congested. Distinguish an accounting threshold from a guarantee of immediate liquidation at a quoted price. The local token and native-coin projects do not provide lending or leverage, so this exercise teaches risk interpretation without connecting a wallet or borrowing real assets.

## Model and assumptions

A happy-path transfer demonstrates one example. An invariant states a property that should hold across an allowed family of transitions, such as conservation of fixed supply or rejection of unauthorized delegated spending. Design tests around the specification, including boundary and failure cases, rather than merely repeating source-code branches.

The project contains deterministic transaction sequences and explicit adverse fixtures. These are not a full fuzzing campaign, formal proof, or external audit. Property-based testing can generate broader sequences, but generators, state models, and coverage still need review. A passing test suite only supports the cases and properties it actually exercises.

$$
fixed\ supply:\sum_i balance_i=S_0
$$

## A worked example

For the fixed-supply contract, the sum of balances among all three fixture accounts remains one million whole tokens after each of twelve transfers. For the native chain, supply changes only by the permitted reward and never exceeds 1,100. A rejected candidate leaves accepted balances, nonces, height, tip, and supply unchanged.

The token test compares compiled runtime with the deployed local runtime and prints source and runtime hashes. The package lock fixes dependency resolution; compiler optimization and EVM target are also part of the build identity.

## Implementation and interpretation

Create a test matrix mapping each promise to at least one positive and one adverse case. Include zero transfer, maximum affordable transfer, overspend, expired authority where implemented, altered signatures, wrong domains, duplicate nonces, and mutation attempts against returned snapshots. Add a self-designed case and explain the expected result before running it. Retain command output and exact source versions. If a new extension changes the invariant, update the specification and tests together rather than weakening an unexplained assertion.

modules.objective: Specify issuance boundaries and distinguish replay recovery from selecting a competing blockchain history.
modules.reading: Unit 6 applied study. Read the primary references, reproduce the worked case, and record the assignment evidence in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A monetary policy must define initial allocation, the schedule of new issuance, rounding, caps, and any authority that can change those rules. In the native lab, genesis creates 1,000 units and each accepted block adds up to ten until supply reaches 1,100. There are no transaction fees or burns. This makes every supply change traceable to a specific accepted block.

Recovery from stored accepted blocks differs from resolving a fork. Replaying one known history can reconstruct deterministic state. Choosing between competing histories requires a consensus rule and evidence that this lab deliberately does not implement. A backup of balances alone also omits the transaction history needed to independently validate those balances.

$$
reward_h=\min(10,1100-S_{h-1})
$$

## A worked example

At heights zero, five, ten, and eleven, the stipulated supplies are 1,000, 1,050, 1,100, and 1,100. Once the cap is reached, further accepted blocks have reward zero. The cap test mines beyond this boundary to show that the implementation stops issuance.

A fresh instance initialized with the same genesis recipient can replay the accepted block sequence and reproduce balances and nonces. A different genesis produces a different initial commitment and cannot silently accept the old history as its own.

## Implementation and interpretation

Write a policy table and test the first block, last positive reward, first zero reward, and a forged excessive reward. Design a hypothetical persistence format with version, genesis identity, accepted blocks, and integrity checks, while documenting that durable storage is not supplied by the exercise. Explain how a future protocol change would affect compatibility and who would have to adopt it. Do not equate editing a local constant with changing the policy of an established public network.

## Model and assumptions

A release artifact should let another reviewer establish what code was built, what code executed, and what behavior was tested. Include source, dependency lock, compiler and EVM settings, constructor arguments, artifact hashes, and test results. A contract address by itself does not communicate all these facts. On a public chain, source verification and deployment identity would require additional independently checked evidence.

For the local course, the deliverable is the supplied archive plus your annotated source, local output, and an authority matrix. The token has constructor-only fixed issuance and no owner or upgrade mechanism. Describe absent powers explicitly in that matrix without claiming that every ERC-20 has the same constraints.

$$
artifact\ identity=(source,dependencies,compiler,settings,constructor)
$$

## A worked example

The initial one-million-token supply remains fixed after transfers and finite delegated spending. The test records metadata, allowance reduction, rejected overspending, conservation, and a runtime-byte match. These connect the specific compiled wrapper to its local observed behavior.

Changing a constructor supply, a dependency version, or compiler settings creates a new build context. Reusing an old report without rerunning the relevant checks would misrepresent which artifact was evaluated.

## Implementation and interpretation

Create a manifest that a peer can follow from a clean extraction using npm ci and npm test. Separate stable expectations such as supply and decimals from varying local account addresses. Include the external dependency's name, version, and license attribution; do not present inherited implementation as wholly original Quanta code. Record known omissions such as no public network, external integration, or independent audit. The course's source references support attribution, while the actual dependency license governs reuse of that dependency.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A working contract is one component of an asset proposal. A public proposal also needs a clear purpose, participant rights or their absence, issuance and allocation rules, controller powers, dependencies, operational responsibilities, and evidence supporting technical claims. A token's name, website, or source citation does not establish permission to reuse another project's assets or imply endorsement.

This course does not conduct a token sale or publish to a public network. Your assignment is a review packet with explicit unresolved decisions. Jurisdiction-specific obligations, permissions, and representations require appropriate current review for the actual activity and participants; a generic course checklist cannot decide them.

$$
\sum_i allocation_i=100\%
$$

## A worked example

Consider a proposal allocating 50% to community use, 20% to a treasury, 20% to contributors, and 10% to liquidity purposes. The percentages sum to 100%, but that arithmetic does not establish whether custody, vesting, distribution, or liquidity mechanisms exist. Each allocation needs a controller, timing rule, and evidence.

A document saying no administrator can mint is inconsistent with code exposing an unrestricted mint role. The review must reconcile prose with reachable authority rather than accepting the more attractive description.

## Implementation and interpretation

Prepare a source and rights register for code, text, images, datasets, and names actually used. Preserve required dependency notices and label original teaching material. Add a claims table with supporting evidence, limitations, and an owner responsible for updates. Record governance changes and incident communication procedures as design requirements. A readiness decision should remain deferred when a material authority, source-rights, security, or operational question is unresolved; passing the course exam does not resolve those questions.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Machine learning estimates a relationship from examples; a trading system additionally needs a decision rule, execution assumptions, and operational controls. Start with the prediction question, horizon, eligible universe, available information, loss function, and baseline. Distinguish forecasting a return, classifying its sign, ranking stocks, and deciding whether an opportunity is worth its costs.

The lifecycle links problem definition to collection, cleaning, features, labels, splitting, training, selection, independent evaluation, error diagnosis, artifact release, inference, monitoring, and retirement. A failure in an early stage can invalidate a sophisticated model later.

$$
y_t=O_{t+2}/O_{t+1}-1
$$

## A worked example

The downloadable project observes features after close t, predicts the return from open t+1 to open t+2, and separately classifies whether that return is positive. With entry 100 and exit 102, its regression target is .02 and its direction label is positive. A positive label alone does not establish profit after execution costs.

## Implementation and interpretation

Create a one-page contract before running the lab. Define what a prediction means and what evidence would reject the idea. Preserve a simple mean-return and class-prior baseline. The default project uses synthetic data and produces research artifacts, not orders. Its negative or inconclusive results are legitimate outcomes of the lifecycle, not reasons to change the test retrospectively.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Financial observations have multiple timestamps: the economic period, exchange event time, publication time, vendor receipt, and later revision time. A statement about last quarter was not necessarily available at quarter end. A historical study should use the version available at its decision cutoff or disclose that a point-in-time reconstruction is unavailable.

Universe membership also changes. Restricting historical training to today's surviving listings can omit delisted or failed firms. Symbols can change and need stable identity mapping. Data access and reuse conditions belong in the source manifest alongside coverage and adjustment conventions.

$$
availableAt\le decisionAt
$$

## A worked example

A filing describes a quarter ending March 31 but is released May 10. A model deciding April 15 cannot use that release merely because its period label says March. Similarly, a record arriving at 21:05 is late for a stipulated 21:00 decision cutoff.

## Implementation and interpretation

The local CSV schema includes date, symbol, open, close, volume, and available_at. It rejects rows unavailable by its synthetic 21:00 UTC cutoff. This clock is a teaching convention, not a real exchange calendar. For actual research, replace it with the intended venue's sessions, publication rules, and dated membership before making historical claims. Record missing coverage explicitly instead of inferring availability from a populated table.

Use the first eight minutes to read the explanation and the linked primary material, then spend eight minutes reproducing and changing the worksheet calculation. Use the remaining fourteen minutes to complete the assignment in your lifecycle notebook or downloaded project. ## Model and assumptions

Cleaning begins with a data contract, not a command that drops every row containing a null. Validate required columns, identifier/date uniqueness, numeric types, units, price positivity, volume conventions, and timestamp availability. Exact duplicate rows can be removed under an explicit policy; conflicting rows for the same date and symbol need a revision rule rather than an arbitrary keep-last choice.

A missing optional volume feature differs from an invalid tradable price. The project preserves missing volume for training-only imputation, while it excludes nonpositive prices and late observations. Every exclusion is counted in the audit so learners can detect unexpected changes in coverage.

$$
retained=raw-exactDuplicates-excludedUniqueRows
$$

## A worked example

Suppose 101 input rows contain one exact duplicate and two distinct invalid-price rows, with no overlap. Removing them leaves 98 rows. A separate missing-volume value can remain in those rows for later imputation; it need not reduce the count to 97.

## Implementation and interpretation

Run the project and inspect audit fields rather than only the cleaned file. Add a conflicting duplicate and verify that the cleaner asks for a defined policy by raising an error. Add a negative price, a nonnumeric volume, and an unknown availability time separately. Keep a copy of raw input and a reproducible transformation history. Never repair a negative price by taking its absolute value without evidence of the source error.

modules.title: Repair missing data, outliers, and corporate-action discontinuities
modules.subtitle: Choose defensible repair or exclusion policies without erasing real market events or introducing future information.
modules.objective: Choose defensible repair or exclusion policies without erasing real market events or introducing future information.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

An extreme observation can be a source error, a split, a stale quote, or a genuine market jump. These cases have different meanings. Compare raw and adjusted fields, volume, corporate-action records, and neighboring observations before choosing a repair. A model may be harmed by a real jump, but removing it solely because it hurts performance changes the research population.

Forward filling an optional slowly changing field can be defensible only with a known availability and staleness rule. Backfilling from a later release uses future information. Tradable prices and target returns should not be invented merely to keep every row in the training matrix.

$$
q_{after}P_{after}=q_{before}P_{before}\quad\text{for the idealized split}
$$

## A worked example

Ten shares priced at 100 become twenty at 50 in a two-for-one split, preserving value 1,000 before other changes. Treating the raw price change as a −50% economic return creates a false label. Conversely, a genuine fall from 100 to 50 without a split is not repaired by doubling the price.

## Implementation and interpretation

The synthetic project has no real corporate-action feed and makes no automatic split repair. It removes bad prices and preserves the global observed date grid so feature and target windows do not silently jump across an excluded observation. Add an audit note distinguishing a confirmed correction from a sensitivity-based exclusion. Fit clipping thresholds, if justified, on training data only and report the number and type of observations changed.

Use the remaining fourteen minutes to complete the assignment in your lifecycle notebook or downloaded project. modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A feature is a dated transformation with a unit, lookback, minimum history, and availability rule. Momentum, rolling volatility, volume transformations, and fundamental ratios can be useful candidates, but their definitions must remain identical in training and inference. Group by stable security identity before shifting or rolling so one stock's last row cannot become another stock's lag.

A lag is only meaningful relative to a calendar. Removing a missing row and shifting the remaining rows can turn a one-session label into a longer interval. The project reindexes each stock to the observed global date grid and requires complete price windows for its five-period features.

$$
momentum_{5,t}=C_t/C_{t-5}-1
$$

## A worked example

A five-period close ratio from 100 to 105 gives momentum .05. A feature based on the close at t is available for the project's after-close decision, but not necessarily for an order assumed to have filled at that same close. Execution timing remains part of the contract.

## Implementation and interpretation

Inspect momentum_5, volatility_5, and log_volume in dataset.csv. Select one row and reconstruct the exact source window. Alter only later prices in a copy and verify that earlier features do not change. For a fundamental extension, perform an as-of join on availability time within the stock and apply an explicit staleness tolerance. Do not join on accounting period alone.

modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A target describes the outcome the model should estimate. A next-close return, next-open holding return, market-relative return, and binary profitable-trade label are different tasks. Costs can be included in a target or in a later decision rule, but the convention must be consistent and clearly named.

Future labels are allowed in historical supervised training only after those outcomes become available. Retain label_end so a training cutoff can exclude labels that extend into validation or test. At inference time, the newest rows have no matured label; they still need features and predictions without inventing outcomes.

$$
class_t=\mathbb{1}[O_{t+2}/O_{t+1}-1>0]
$$

## A worked example

At decision t, the next two opening prices are 200 and 198. The project's target is −1% and the positive-sign class is false. If the previous close was 190, using 198/190−1 would define a different interval and falsely include a price move that the stipulated next-open entry did not capture.

## Implementation and interpretation

Open dataset.csv and verify the entry/exit prices for one positive and one negative row. Keep the last unresolved label rows out of training while allowing them in the separate scoring feature path. If adding multi-day or barrier labels, store actual end times and reconsider overlap, class balance, costs, and purging. Do not select the horizon solely because it produces the best final test chart.

modules.subtitle: Create train, validation, and test partitions that respect financial chronology and label availability.
modules.objective: Create train, validation, and test partitions that respect financial chronology and label availability.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

Random row splitting can place the same market date or overlapping outcome interval in both training and evaluation. For the pooled stock task here, split by global date so all stocks on a date receive the same partition. Keep model selection in validation and reserve test for a frozen procedure.

The project uses approximately 60%, 20%, and 20% of eligible dates. It purges earlier rows whose label_end reaches the next partition's start. This is stricter than merely checking the feature date. A separate development set combines eligible pre-test observations for a final refit after validation selection.

$$
train_i\ eligible\iff decision_i<cutoff\land labelEnd_i<cutoff
$$

## A worked example

If validation starts at index 10 and each label ends two indices after its observation, training observations 8 and 9 are excluded: their labels end at 10 and 11. Observation 7 ends at 9 and can qualify. A long irregular label could require an even earlier exclusion.

## Implementation and interpretation

Inspect report.json split boundaries and assert last training label end is before the first validation decision, and last development label end is before the first test decision. Verify no date appears in two decision partitions. For multi-asset event data, also consider shared events and issuer relationships where they affect the intended generalization claim. Chronology alone does not solve every dependence or selection problem, so state what population the split is designed to represent.

modules.subtitle: Keep preprocessing statistics within the training fit and reuse exactly those transformations for validation, test, and inference.
modules.objective: Keep preprocessing statistics within the training fit and reuse exactly those transformations for validation, test, and inference.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A transformation can learn from data even when it has no target variable. Medians, means, standard deviations, clipping quantiles, PCA components, and feature selections all carry sample information. Fitting them on the complete dataset exposes the training procedure to held-out observations. A pipeline keeps the transformation and estimator in one fit/predict contract.

The project uses median imputation, standardization, and an estimator. Optional missing volume is handled by the fitted imputer; invalid price and target windows have already been excluded. Validation and test call predict, not fit_transform, on this pipeline.

$$
z=(x-\mu_{train})/\sigma_{train}
$$

## A worked example

Training values [1,2,9] have median 2. A missing validation value should receive that fitted median, even if later values would make the full-sample median much larger. For a feature with training mean 10 and scale 2, an observed value 14 becomes standardized value 2.

## Implementation and interpretation

Inspect the imputer statistics and scaler means in the fitted artifact. Change only held-out feature values and refit on the unchanged training slice; training statistics must remain identical. When a model is legitimately refitted on the larger pre-test development set, its preprocessing may change because its authorized training population changed. Document that distinction so a valid final refit is not confused with accidental test leakage.

modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

A regression model estimates a numerical target under a chosen loss. Mean squared error emphasizes large residuals, while mean absolute error has a different sensitivity. A constant prediction based on the training mean is a useful baseline for squared error; using the test mean instead would give the baseline information unavailable at deployment.

Ridge regression adds a coefficient penalty to least squares. The penalty trades fit against coefficient magnitude and can stabilize correlated predictors. Its scale depends on the objective convention and feature scaling, so record the implementation and preprocessing. A smaller training error alone does not establish a better future model.

$$
MSE=n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Predictions [1,2,3] and outcomes [1,3,5] have errors [0,1,2], MSE 5/3, and MAE 1 in the stated units. If a training-mean baseline has MSE 2, the model improves this particular error comparison by 1−(5/3)/2≈16.7%.

## Implementation and interpretation

Run the project's three ridge candidates and retain every validation loss. Compare the selected model's held-out error with mean_baseline_mse. Inspect the fitted coefficient scale only after accounting for standardization. Do not interpret a coefficient as a causal effect or a return guarantee. Record a negative result when the baseline wins and identify whether the next justified experiment concerns data, target, features, or model assumptions.

## Model and assumptions

Logistic regression models a binary outcome through a probability link. The class definition comes first: the project labels a positive next-open holding return, not a profitable trade after every cost. A probability estimate and a hard decision threshold are separate outputs. Class imbalance can make raw accuracy misleading because predicting the majority class may already score well.

The project fits logistic candidates on training data, compares validation Brier loss, and refits the selected configuration on eligible development observations. A fixed .55 threshold is declared for the confusion matrix; it is not optimized on test results.

$$
precision=TP/(TP+FP),\quad recall=TP/(TP+FN)
$$

## A worked example

If only 20 of 100 outcomes are positive, predicting negative for every row achieves 80% accuracy and zero positive recall. If a classifier accepts ten opportunities and six are positive, precision is .6; if twenty positives existed, recall is .3. Neither statistic alone describes the magnitude of gains and losses.

## Implementation and interpretation

Inspect class counts in each date partition before fitting. A training slice with only one class cannot support the intended logistic fit. Compare probabilities with the development class-prior baseline, and retain confusion counts rather than only a headline score. If using weighting or resampling, apply it within training and re-evaluate calibration and the population being represented. Do not balance the final test by deleting inconvenient real outcomes.

## Model and assumptions

A decision tree partitions feature space into regions. Deep trees can fit highly specific patterns, while ensembles combine multiple trees using different construction rules. Random forests average randomized trees; boosting adds models sequentially to improve an objective. Their hyperparameters and uncertainty properties differ, so do not treat all tree ensembles as interchangeable.

The downloadable project trains a bounded random forest candidate with a fixed seed, depth, leaf size, and tree count. It compares that candidate with ridge using the same training and validation observations. Gradient boosting is a documented extension exercise, not a hidden implementation in the supplied run.

$$
ensemble\ prediction=B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}f_b(x)\quad\text{for an averaging ensemble}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose ridge validation MSE is .00018 and a forest's is .00016, while their training errors are .00015 and .00003. The forest wins this stipulated validation comparison, but its very low training error alone would not justify selection. The final independent result may still favor the simpler baseline.

Inspect the candidate definition and validation trial ledger. Change one complexity parameter in a new development experiment, record the added trial, and compare both training and validation behavior. Keep missing-data handling and feature definitions consistent. If adding boosting, disable or carefully control any internal validation scheme that violates the time contract. Record runtime and memory as engineering costs alongside statistical performance.

## Model and assumptions

A neural network composes learned transformations under an optimization objective. Hidden width, depth, regularization, learning rate, batch construction, and stopping criteria influence both capacity and training behavior. More parameters do not create information absent from the features or repair mislabeled outcomes. A small tabular baseline remains a useful reference even when sequence architectures are being considered.

Sequence windows introduce additional alignment and overlap requirements. The last input timestamp must precede the decision cutoff, while the target interval must remain separate. Randomly distributing overlapping windows across partitions can share substantial historical information and outcome structure.

$$
dense\ parameters=n_{in}n_{out}+n_{out}
$$

## A worked example

A dense layer with three inputs and four hidden units has 3×4 weights and four biases, totaling sixteen parameters. A single output connected to those four units adds five, for twenty-one in this small two-layer example. This count describes capacity, not the number of independent financial observations.

## Implementation and interpretation

Design a local MLPRegressor extension using the primary documentation and the existing pipeline interface. Keep the parameter budget small, seed recorded, scaling fitted within training, and validation chronological. The supplied default project does not train a neural model; your extension must produce its own trial and convergence evidence. Compare runtime, validation loss, and sensitivity with ridge and forest before claiming that a larger sequence model is warranted.

## Model and assumptions

Every tried feature set, hyperparameter, seed choice, and stopping rule is part of the research search. A small declared candidate set is easier to audit than an undocumented sequence of improvements. Record the primary validation metric and tie-breaking rule before fitting. The best validation result is selected evidence, not an untouched estimate of future performance.

The project implements a single chronological train/validation/test design. Walk-forward and nested designs are extensions: repeat the selection procedure within each outer training history, then evaluate its frozen choice on the next dated block. Do not describe the supplied single split as a full nested backtest.

$$
\hat\lambda=\arg\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda}L_{validation}(\lambda)
$$

## A worked example

Three candidates have validation losses .020, .018, and .021. The second wins the declared minimum-loss rule. If the researcher then sees a poor final test and adds a fourth candidate tailored to it, that test has become development evidence. A new independent evaluation or an explicit limitation is needed.

Save the full trial ledger and split manifest. Use the advanced research lab's interval-purged splits as a starting point for a three-origin extension, but fit preprocessing and model selection afresh within each permitted history. Aggregate losses with declared date/row weighting and report variation across origins. Record computational budget and failed fits rather than silently dropping them from the comparison.

modules.content:
## Model and assumptions

MSE and MAE evaluate numerical prediction errors in different ways. R-squared compares squared error with variation around the evaluated sample mean and can be negative. An out-of-sample improvement against an available training-mean baseline is a related but distinct comparison. Classification metrics such as ROC AUC and average precision assess ordering under different summaries; neither directly measures tradable profit.

Precision and recall require their denominators. When no positives are predicted, precision is undefined under the project's convention. A one-class evaluation slice also cannot supply ordinary two-class ROC AUC. Reporting null with a reason is more informative than fabricating a perfect score.

$$
relative\ MSE\ improvement=1-MSE_{model}/MSE_{baseline}
$$

## A worked example

A model MSE .8 against an available baseline MSE 1 gives a 20% relative improvement. A classifier with TP=8, FP=2, and FN=12 has precision .8 and recall .4. The high precision does not show that it found most positives or that its positive predictions had favorable payoff magnitudes.

## Implementation and interpretation

Read the project's full held-out metric report and compare every model metric with the appropriate baseline. Reconstruct confusion counts and verify they sum to the test sample size. Add a per-date or per-stock error table to detect domination by a large subgroup. Do not choose the final headline metric after discovering which makes the model look strongest; distinguish exploratory summaries from the metric declared in the contract.
